New shares are sold at one price, the last trade or fair value before one, and never through the book, because a plan needs to know in the month it builds what it raised. The city's fund never subscribes (0.7.14).

**Forty percent of a positive month is paid out**, from the till, or from the company's own money abroad if the till is short — since 0.7.11 of what the month's net income leaves once the principal it repaid is taken off, Jerus: *"Pay out after principal"*, and since 0.7.12 of that principal net of the new borrowing that rolled it, which is free cash flow to equity, the figure real companies pay dividends from. The bank pays by its own rule ([the bank](#13-the-bank)). A company's **fair value** is the higher of its book equity and the dividend it actually pays capitalised at the world's required return, per share; its **price** is its last trade, and before its first trade its fair value.

### One book for each company

Jerus: *"Order book for both."* Since 0.7.12 every share that changes hands meets its buyer on an order book (`OrderBook`), one per company: price and then time decide who is filled, a trade is at the resting order's price, nobody trades with themselves, and **nobody is obliged to trade** — an order with nobody across it rests, and every order still resting is withdrawn at the month's step and posted again from each participant's view of the new month. Each participant posts from the rule it already followed, in this order:

- **The bank's desk**, if it has capital: a bid one per cent under fair value for what its capital can carry, an ask one per cent over it for what it holds, and an ask at fair value itself for anything past its two caps — 25% of the bank's equity in any one company and 50% in all of them. Its own shares are capital, not trading: it bids for them only with what it holds over its target and sells new ones only while it is under it.
- **Emigrants** sell on the way out, and what nobody bids for stays abroad with them.
- **The world** buys when the dividend yield at the best ask clears its own rate plus a three-point premium by a margin, and sells into strength when it falls short, never into a crash, and never in a company under a year old.
- **Companies** past their first year and not in a bad one, with more equity than their target and six months of their costs and their debt service in the till bid for their own shares at up to 10% over fair value, a tenth of the company a year at most, and cancel what they buy. What nobody sells them **stays in the company**: no special dividend is paid by any path since 0.7.12, because paying the unspent money out left the tills bare and brought the failures back.
- **Every household cell** is a participant of its own (Jerus: *"Each household type trades"*): a cell under its cushion offers a tenth of the shortfall at the market, and a cell past it buys four per cent of its excess a month into the best yield over the bank's deposit rate plus a point, the pace its dollars abroad move at.
- **The city's fund** last, taking what the others left, at fair value ([tax, policy and GDP](#11-tax-policy--gdp)).

A household short of money sells in the middle of the month, in its waterfall, at the price at which the dividend it gives up costs what borrowing would, so the rich cells' resting bids are where a poor cell's shares go — a transfer between households that no audited pool sees. A share priced at a hundred times its founding price is split a hundred for one, and one that falls to a hundredth is consolidated, and every holding, every resting order and the last trade move by the factor; a cumulative split factor keeps the price history readable per founding share. On the default seed on 28 September the book traded $39.2bn of shares in 44,049 trades over 4,002 months, a listed company traded in 46% of its months, and the median last trade stood at 0.99 of fair value.

### The bank was the dealer, until 0.7.12

From the exchange's first night until 0.7.12 the bank's trading desk was the counterparty on every trade, and quoted nothing when the bank was dead. It quoted around fair value, its own book moved the quote, it never sold what it did not hold, and it marked what it held at the lower of the quote and fair value. Its book was capped at a multiple of the bank's equity, which is money — and until 18 September that cap was the one figure in the exchange a currency reform did not divide. It was re-struck each month *after* the households settled, so for the first half of every month a reformed city's desk believed it had a hundred times the room it had; a household with no savings and a grocery bill it could not meet borrowed in the plain city and sold $1.03 of shares in the reformed one, and from there household debt was 4.2% apart in one month and the exchange rate with it. The bisect blamed the fourteenth sector's inventory term, and the term was right: it had moved GDP, GDP had moved what the desk's book was worth against its limit, and a cancellation that had been landing on one side of zero started landing on the other. A bisect names what perturbed a fault, not what the fault is; a latent member of that family is not a harmless one, it is one nobody has perturbed yet.

```
mid = fair × clamp(1 − 0.25 × (dealerShares − demand) / scale, 0.50, 5.00)     // the dealer's quote, until 0.7.12
bid/ask = mid ∓ half of a 2% spread
```

**The desk foots, since 19 September.** Its opened lines on the bank's statement had left out the term that is usually the largest — the change in the mark on what it holds — so a loss sat over sub-lines that did not add to it. *Re-marked what it holds* (`Bank.getMarkChange()`) is a line of its own now, and when it is the bulk of a loss the note says why, which is Jerus's question — *"explain to me the trading desk, cause a bunch of times it's losing billions"*: with buyers it could not fill the dealer quoted up to five times fair value to draw sellers, and it marked what it held at the lower of the quote and fair value, so a wave of emigrants selling into a bubble cost it the difference the same day. `BankCheck` asserts the lines plus the re-mark equal the total, and on a played city they did in 120 of 120 months. Whether a dealer should bid at a quote it does not believe in stopped being a question when the dealer went; the desk marks at the lower of the last trade and fair value. Since 0.7.1 the same desk also buys back the city's paper from the households, at the month's market value off the curve.

> **What it was worth**
>
> When the exchange arrived, eight seeds against the batch before it: GDP $65M → $77M a month, worst unemployment 46% → 37%, exports $104M → $124M, the currency inside 3.5% of parity, dividends to households $3–18bn → $30–56bn a run, every company home-owned in six seeds of eight — and **bank failures 10 → 0**, because the trading desk was a business and a profitable one, and a sector that has just paid its owners borrows for its next mine.

### The firms sell bonds

Jerus: *"notes are the loans businesses make to the banks, and bonds are debts that they issue to investors… households can buy them, but banks also buy them as, only if it wants, and yes they are tradeable so they have par value and all."* The bank failed 115 times on 0.7.11's eight default seeds, and the cause was concentration: the one bank was every business's only lender, and the sector that broke it owed five to six times its equity. So since 0.7.12 a sector borrows through two doors. A **bond** (`CorporateBond`) is a ten-year bullet with a coupon every month, built at par: the underwriter announces the room, every bidder says what it would take at each yield, the coupon is the lowest yield that fills the issue and the rest is a bank loan, and the bank underwrites it for the city's own charge, $12k plus 0.75%. A sector borrowing for a building takes the largest bond whose all-in cost is no dearer than the loan and borrows the rest; the first reading let bonds raise what a capital-short bank had refused, at coupons up to 16%, and failed the bank more, so loan and bond together never pass what the bank would lend. A sector short in the month can be sold a bond by the shortfall desk the same way.

Every bond trades on a book of its own, and the buyers are the ones Jerus named, each by the rule it already had for the nearest thing it holds: the household cells by their rule for the city's paper, wanting a share of each issue that rises with its expected return over what savers are paid; companies that owe nothing by the rule that sends idle cash abroad, never into their own bonds; the world by hot money's; the bank only on the capital it holds over its target, at the yield that makes the bond earn what an equal loan would; and the city's fund. A household short of money sells its bonds after its dollars abroad and before its shares. A bond that falls due is paid from its issuer's till to every holder at face. When a sector's firms default the bondholders lose too, and since 0.7.12 each instrument recovers what it recovers in the world: 75% of a bank loan and 45% of a bond (`LOAN_RECOVERY`, `BOND_RECOVERY`, the midpoints of Moody's and S&P's long-run averages), and the eight seeds measured 74.8% and 44.9%. On the default seed on 28 September 2,266 bonds were issued for $71.2bn over the run; 44 were outstanding at the end, $2.36bn, the households holding $1.29bn of it, other companies $914M and the world $126M.

The player does not trade, bar the fund's hand. The Sector page's *Its owners* block shows the last trade and its month, or fair value where there has been none, the yield on the dividend actually paid, the month's trades, and five levels of bids and asks with the company's own buyback resting among them; there is a price chart per company, each household cell's shares at the last trade and its bonds, the foreign share of each register on the balance-of-payments page, and under Finances a bond market with every issue, who holds it and each bond's own book twelve levels deep.

## 10. Labour & schools

*A wage used to be one of six constants, copied in once at startup. Labour is a market now, skill is an axis, and a school is the only way to make a doctor at home.*

### Four bands, one price each

```
NONE < DIPLOMA < COLLEGE < UNIVERSITY       // substitution runs downward only
tightness = posts / qualified supply        // per band; a band's surplus cascades into the one below
target    = minimumWage × ratio[job] × clamp(tightness^0.5, 0.70, 4.0)
wage     += (target − wage) × 0.12          // 90% of a shortage prices in over 18 months
```

The **minimum wage is the base** of the whole ladder, so one Policy dial moves every wage in the city, the treasury's own payroll included. Because the unskilled base *is* the floor, an unskilled glut cannot be priced away — it clears in people instead, which is exactly what a binding minimum wage does. Wages also chase the cost of living in full, both directions, over 24 months, and since 0.6.11 a harness holds them to it: `LabourCheck` runs 240 months of steady inflation and asserts every month that the wage index moves exactly `DRIFT_PER_MONTH` of the way toward the published price index, through a currency reform and a reload, and on all eight seeds every one of 144 checkpoint readings sits at the level the two-year lag implies — the one-third overshoot measured on 15 September does not reproduce. Students and prisoners are out of the supply while they are away, and the pool is what is left when filled posts are taken off the labour force — an identity, not a second count.

**Gated jobs carry a licence premium** on top of their band's: posts over licence holders, same elasticity, never below one, the pair capped at 4×. A hospital with no medical school pays its doctors over the graduate band — measured at 1.26× against a band in glut at 0.83× — and that price is what draws licensed arrivals and sends graduates back to school.

### Nine schools, and a pipeline

| Stage | Takes | Produces | Course |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| Elementary, Middle, High | children and teens | a diploma, at the *narrowest* stage's coverage | 4 + 3 + 5 yr |
| Community College | diploma-holders | college graduates | 24 mo |
| University | diploma-holders | university graduates | 48 mo |
| Medical, Law, Business, Technology | university graduates | a licence for one job type — raises nobody's band | 84 / 36 / 24 / 48 mo |

Three things make an adult study, multiplied not averaged: a free seat, a return (nobody spends four years to earn what they already earn — a medical student's alternative is the best *ungated* university job), and the money, with tuition a Policy dial between the treasury and the household. **Students are in flight**: cohorts queue by months remaining, graduate at the front, thin at the adults' own attrition, and are out of the labour supply until they finish — living on savings, a grant worth $525 a month at the default dial, and a loan they begin repaying over 114 months the month they graduate. A university built today is graduates in month 49, not this month. Migration can still bring a licensed professional — some share of arriving graduates already hold one — so a small city imports its doctor and a city of eighty thousand cannot import two hundred at any price. That is the handoff to the schools, by arithmetic rather than by rule.

### The price of a place

Jerus: *"grants its just a menu where you can choose between a fixed amount, or a percentage of last month's surplus, or a % as it is now of living costs, or a % of tuition. and then another slider which is the interest rate for the student loans … and also make it so that you can tweak the price of tuition as well."* Since 0.6.9 the Policy tab's *Promises → Schools* page — the Tuition page renamed — has carried the students' dials on one foot bar: five when it opened, and since 0.7.6 a price for each kind of school besides. **The grant is a basis and an amount** (`TaxPolicy.GrantBasis`): a share of the unskilled wage, which is the founding rule and the default, and which is what "as it is now of living costs" turned out to be; a fixed sum a student; a share of last month's surplus, as one pool; or a share of each student's own course fee. Each basis has its own ceiling, and all four are struck by one rule, `TaxPolicy.grantBill`, that the treasury's bill, the save's re-strike, the students' row and the page all call, so a grant on the wrong thing cannot look right on one screen and wrong on another. **The student loan has a rate**, 0 to 15%, nothing by default: the Canadian shape, nothing accruing while they study, charged on a graduate's balance and paid with the instalment, so the balance is only ever principal and falls exactly as it did. The interest is the treasury's own revenue line, *Student loan interest*; the principal still comes back through the treasury's journal. A prisoner's loan freezes with the rest of their debts, no instalment and no interest. **And the price of a place is the player's**: `tuitionScale`, 0 to 5× the founding table, read wherever a fee is read.

**Since 0.7.6 it is a price per school.** Jerus: *"have it so that not only can you raise prices but also raise the price for a specific university, and beside the dial it shows the current space, the current students, and the current cost and revenue."* The scale is nine, one for each kind of school (`TaxPolicy.tuitionScaleOf(type)`), in the shape 0.7.4 gave the income taxes: *Every school at once* sits at the top of the page and moves all nine, and taking it back unstages every kind's own; under it is a row per kind with its own dial and four figures off the model — the places its buildings seat, the students in it, what its staff and buildings cost the treasury this month, and the tuition its students paid. A kind with nothing standing says *no school* and its dial is greyed. The nine ride the end of the policy array, and a shorter array reads them as the one scale it carried. Building it found the trap 0.7.4 had found for the income tax: the month and the load path told every school the first kind's price, which would have put nine prices back to one on every load, and `Game.tellTheSchoolsTheirPrices` hands each kind its own now.

At the defaults nothing moves, bit for bit. At ×3 the poverty trap the `Education` header describes is back: a one-university city at five years has 1,718 students and 69% of its diploma-holders willing at ×1, 1,173 and 26% at ×3, and 1,756 and 90% at ×0. The default playtest has never built a school, so `-Dplaytest.schools=true` builds them, and eight seeds at tuition ×3, the grant half of tuition and loans at 5% all ran clean, the treasury taking $1.1–3.8M a month of interest and fewer people studying. On the way the schools' books were found never to have been restored on the load path — the sixth sighting of that gap, fixed.

## 11. Tax, policy & GDP

*Four base rates since 0.7.4 — on profit, on sales, on wages and on property — and everything else is an offset in rate points from one of them. Resolution happens in one place, clamped, so no screen can quote a rate the city does not collect.*

| Lever | Default | Max | Offsets |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Profit tax | 15% | 60% | fifteen sectors; the bank is charged retail's rate |
| Sales tax | 15% | 60% | fifteen sectors |
| Wage tax | 15% | 60% | four education wage bands |
| Property tax | 1.5%/yr | 10%/yr | fifteen sectors, plus farmland relief; quoted annually, charged monthly |

Beside them: the minimum wage, the policy interest rate, tuition's split and since 0.6.9 its price, the pension contribution and replacement rates, the EI premium and benefit rates, the students' grant on its basis and the student loan's rate, since 0.6.8 the health fee's scale and the health premium, since 16 September the transit fare, and since 0.7.14 the city's fund's dial — each a dial with a stated maximum. The rollover and what happens when the bank fails are the treasury's settings, on Finances ([the city's borrowing](#12-the-citys-borrowing), [the bank](#13-the-bank)). The fare is the one that is a price rather than a charge: it is set per ride, $2.50 by default and $50 at the absurd end, and charged forty journeys a month, because a rider is a person and for its first day it was charged once a month against a constant that says *a single journey*. Jerus caught it by reading the number.

**The policy rate reaches 100% since 0.7.2** (`DebtManager.MAX_POLICY_RATE` 1.00; it stopped at 25% before), a bound that never binds in play and is there so a typo cannot set 2,500%. The slider has chips at 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50, 75 and 100. The Taylor rule beside it is printed as the rule says it (`ruleRate()`), and where the dial's bounds cut it the page says so: *"the rule would set −4.60%, the dial stops at 0.00%"* was the default seed's last month on 22 September, on −3.1% inflation, and on 28 September it read −0.35% on −0.2%. Since 0.7.0 the dial is the price of money, and it has three companions on the same page: the target the rule aims at, a dial since 0.7.4, the holdings dial and the advances ceiling; all four are told in [the central bank](#14-the-central-bank).

### Setting them: five pages, one proposal

"Income tax" is not one tax. It is three — on profit, on value added, and on every payroll — and until 0.7.4 the three shared one dial, and the screens used to be split by *where the modifier lived* rather than by what the money is. They are split by the tax now: Everything · Profit · Sales · Wage · Property. Jerus: *"sure you can choose sale tax for manufacturing, but what about just increasing sale tax for all at the same time? currently that's a hassle, i want to be able to do that for every type of tax, even wage tax."* Since 0.7.4 each of the three has a base of its own, every offset rides its own tax's base, and each tax page's top dial is that base; the old city rate is *Every tax at once* on the Everything page, which moves all three and shows the three side by side. Splitting them found the load path reading the old single rate *after* the policy array, which would have put a split back together on every load, and the Government tab printing the bank's profit tax at the income rate while the city charged it retail's.

```
[−]  ══════●══════  [+]        20.25%
0.00% to 60.00% · one step is 0.25 points · it is 20.00%
```

Drag to cross the range; it snaps hard on release, and each button is worth exactly one step. **The step is a quarter point everywhere except property, which gets a twentieth** — the same step has a very different bite: 20.00% to 20.25% of income is one part in eighty of what income tax raises, 1.00% to 1.25% of assessed value is one part in four.

**Since 0.7.6 it is every dial's shape, not the tax pages' own.** Jerus: *"all the dials in the policy in the promises section, make them a slider with steps, and a + − on the ends, basically i think it's better if you create an object or class of slider"*. There had been three shapes of one control, and there is one class now, `ui/Ladder`: a minus, a slider that snaps to the step, a plus, the reading in the accent colour when it is off what the city charges, and an ends line — *x to y · one step is z · it is w*. The sensitivity is the step and nothing else, because a drag coarser than a click would be two dials in one. The reading follows the thumb and the change waits for the release, because restaging on every pixel redraws the screen under the pointer. On it are every tax dial and the farmland relief, the wage floor and the policy rate, the target, the holdings and the ceiling, which apply at once and keep their chips as shortcuts, the pension's two, EI's two, both health dials, the tuition split, every school's price, the grant and the loan, and the fare on Services; each kept its key, range, step and formatter exactly, and `PolicyCheck` did not notice. The standing subsidies are switches and the currency reform is a choice of three, so neither is a ladder.

**Changes stage and apply together.** A budget is not one rate moved in isolation, so several dials can be moved and applied as one proposal; the foot bar lists them in the order they were made, and a dial dragged back to the live value unstages rather than staging a no-op. Each dial registers its own setter, which is what lets one bar apply a city rate, three sector offsets and the farmland relief without a switch on the key. The foot bar strikes the same arithmetic twice — once at what the city charges, once at what is staged — and says plainly that *both* figures are models: comparing a model against last month's actual would make a batch that changed nothing read as a swing. The difference is the answer.

The wage page totals what a payslip actually loses — wage tax plus the pension contribution plus the EI premium, and since 0.6.8 the health premium — which no screen in this game had ever added up. The premiums and the contribution are read-only there, with a door to Promises, because a second copy of a lever is how two screens start disagreeing about what the city charges.

### What the treasury actually did

The Government tab has a bridge from the budget balance — an income measure — to what the treasury's cash actually did between one press and the next, and until 19 September its last row, *Everything else the treasury did*, was a residual with a name on it: land, buildings, reserves, capital put into the bank, bonds bought back, on any month the player did one of them. Jerus: *"it just says 'everything else' — that should be expandable, cause a lot of times that's where a bunch of important things happen."* It opens now. `TreasuryJournal` records every movement of the city's cash that is neither a budget line nor paper raised or repaid, where it happens and in the player's words — *Put capital into the bank*, *Bought reserves*, *Bought back a bond*, *Lent to students, net of repayments*, since 0.7.0 *Repaid the central bank* and *Advanced by the central bank (printed)*, since 0.7.6 land bought out of the vault, and since 0.7.14 what the dial paid into the fund and what resolving the bank cost — press to press, for the month that ended and the one in progress, both carried in the save. What the lines do not explain prints under them as *Not accounted for*, and on a month the city borrows it is the first coupon's timing, to the cent. Land and buildings stay on the budget's own line and are deliberately not named twice. Opening the row found that *Raised by issuing paper* had read $0 on every month the city borrowed, because its counter was cleared before the strike; that the city's own repair bill and the transit fares are on the Government screen and not in the budget's totals, which are journalled by name until they are; and, not fixed that night, that the bank had never paid for the city's paper (see [debt](#12-the-citys-borrowing)). The budget gained its own lines in the batches since — the health premium, student loan interest, the central bank's remittance and the interest on its advances, a Subsidies line the Government tab had never had, since 0.7.11 the premiums the landlords pay to insure their mortgages under revenue and the claims the city pays on them under spending, and since 0.7.14 *Transfer from the fund* — and since 0.7.6 *Land bought* opens into what was converted, what came out of the vault and what was bought back. And since 0.7.0 every payment the treasury makes goes through one door, `Game.treasuryPays(TreasuryLine, amount)`, which is what lets the central bank's ceiling decide who is paid.

### VAT with input credits

Sales tax is a real value-added tax: exports zero-rated with credits still claimable, imports charged at the buyer's rate and fully creditable, the city exempt both ways, residential rent an exempt supply. One deliberate departure from the real thing — **the rate follows the producer, not the product** — because under a product rate most of the sector dials would be cosmetic.

Net remittance is allowed to go negative and is not floored: under producer rates a sector buying high and selling low genuinely is owed money, and flooring would quietly turn a rate cut into a partial one. When it happens the screen names who is owed. **And the producer pays it** — out of its own cash, as it pays the profit tax on its statement's after-tax line. Both used to be collected by the treasury from nobody; closing the money identity found them.

### GDP

Measured by expenditure, C + I + G + NX, replacing an income-approach figure that went negative the moment firms started paying interest. Profit is not production.

```
C  what the households bought over three counters — the grocers', the boutiques', the kitchens' — + rent paid
I  construction work put in place + the change in inventory as a VOLUME, priced today: the food shelf at fixed weights, the makers' materials, the boutiques' stockroom
G  utility payroll + the health service's gross cost + the police's
NX everything sold abroad − everything landed: scrap, food, materials, machinery, vans, watches, and the railway's fuel
```

Inventory is measured as a volume rather than a value, because valuing it books every price move as production — a rule that had to be re-learned the day food became thirteen goods, since the obvious way to add kilograms of grain to kilograms of fish is to value each at its own price. The thirteen are aggregated at *fixed* weights instead, so the figure is still a quantity. The builders' yard is deliberately excluded from the inventory term — work in progress is at contract value and already embodies it, so counting both subtracted the same brick twice — while the materials plant's warehouse is output made and not yet sold, and counts like a mill's. The boutiques' stockroom is the third term, and it was found by a negative month: a Boutique's three months of stock, 960 pieces at $9,000, lands in one month, NX took the landed cost out and nothing said the city still had the goods, so a city that took up shopping reported negative GDP sixty times over a run. Priced at what the shop paid, the arrival nets to zero and the margin is the only thing that scores; sixty negative months became one across eight seeds and 32,040 months. *Any good a sector can hold and does not consume within the month belongs in that block the day the good is written.* A household's car is not in C: a household turning money into a thing it owns is a portfolio move, like a share. Land sales appear in the government's books and *nowhere* in GDP: selling a field moves an asset that already existed, and counting it would let a city manufacture growth by trading land with itself. Education's cost is still outside G, which healthcare's and the police's are not, and the transit payroll joined it on the outside when the modes arrived; that is an inconsistency and it is on the list.

**And since 0.7.6 it can be drawn in its layers.** Jerus: *"have it so the gdp graph can be a toggle, and if toggled it switches from line to mountain graph is it? layered, aka showing how much is made up of investments, net exports, government spending, aka breaking it down."* The four parts are series of their own — `consumption`, `investment`, `government`, `netExports`, each with its rule in the year book and deflated the way real GDP is — and a *layers* chip on the Reports page stacks C, I and G from zero with the real GDP line drawn over them, so the gap between the top of the stack and the line is net exports, above it when the city exports more than it lands and below it when not. A stacked area cannot hold a negative layer, and the caption says so. `HistoryCheck` asserts that the four add up to the month's GDP to the cent.

### Standing subsidies

Any sector can be put under a standing policy that covers its losses exactly, uncapped, month after month. It is booked as a *capital contribution*, not revenue — the sector's cash rises and its income statement still says it lost money. The city goes overdrawn to pay it, and the overdraft — the central bank's advances since 0.7.0 — is priced as debt, so an over-generous policy bills you through the interest rate; and once the advances have reached their ceiling a subsidy is paid only from cash at or above zero, and what it is refused is owed to the sector as arrears.

### The city's fund

Jerus: *"Rule plus your hand"*, and *"Home only"*. Since 0.7.14 the treasury has a fund (`TreasuryFund`), a pool of its own inside the city: a market book of company shares, the bank's among them, and company bonds; a rescue book of a resolved bank's shares, the city's preferred and its warrants ([the bank](#13-the-bank)); and its cash. Its holdings live where everyone else's do, as a city holding on each company's register and a city holder on every bond, and it posts on both books by a rule and, separately, by the player's hand. It never subscribes to a new issue and never buys the city's own paper.

**The dial** takes 0 to 300% of the year's surplus, nothing by default, paid in once a year at December's close and before the rollover nets the same surplus, so that the two cannot spend it twice; a deficit year saves nothing, and past 100% the rest comes out of the treasury's cash but never takes it below a month of its own spending, the liquidity rule Canada keeps and the rollover already reads. Yearly, because a monthly pay-in would save in the good months of a deficit year. **The rule** is Norway's Government Pension Fund Global: 70% shares and 30% bonds, never more than 10% of any company, rebalanced when shares pass 74% or fall more than four points under 70%, every order at fair value, and money that does not fit waits as cash, which earns nothing, as the treasury's does. **The transfer** is Norway's fiscal rule since 2017: 3% a year of everything it holds, a twelfth a month, to the budget as *Transfer from the fund*, from its cash only — the rule never sells to pay it. **The hand** places orders at fair value, good for a month, and may sell any share or bond the fund holds, the rescue book's bank shares included, though not the preferred or its warrants; paying in and drawing out are transfers between two government pools and stay off the budget. The fund has its own area under Finances, *The city's fund*, with a Holdings page and a By hand page.

At the default dial of nothing the default seed on 28 September still ended with a fund of \$116M, fed by the dividends on the bank shares its one resolution had handed it (\$239M of the \$270M of dividends it took), and paid the budget \$659M over the run. On eight seeds at a dial of 100% it was paid \$15.3T and held about 94% of it as cash, and the cities ended at 174,264 people on average against 166,717 at nothing (0.7.14).

## 12. The city's borrowing

*Three instruments with genuinely different shapes, priced off their own cash flows rather than off a formula that assumed a bullet — and since 0.7.1 all three off one curve that sits on the policy dial, held by whoever bought them: the households, the central bank, and the bank for the rest. Since 0.7.13 the treasury can roll what falls due without the player's hand. What lends to everybody else is [the bank](#13-the-bank).*

| Instrument | Duration | Granularity | Shape |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| T-Bill | 3–12 months | $1M | zero coupon, sold at a discount, one lump at maturity; the short end of the curve, at the dial |
| Serial bond | 1–10 years | $10M | monthly coupon on a declining balance, annual principal slices |
| Term bond | 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 years | $100M | low coupon on full face, whole face at maturity |

> **Why the term bond is solved from present value**
>
> The old simple-interest premium made issue-then-repurchase an infinite money button — $2,145 of free cash at ten years, rising to $28,059 at thirty. Solving the face from the bond's present value makes the round trip neutral by construction rather than by a patch.

### The dial, and the curve on it

The **policy rate** is the player's dial on the Policy tab, 0% to 100% since 0.7.2, and since 0.7.0 it is the price of money rather than a floor under somebody else's: the commercial bank's spare cash earns it at the central bank, and its shortfalls pay it and a quarter point at the window ([the central bank](#14-the-central-bank)). The **city's own borrowing rate** is that dial — never less than what the money costs the bank that buys the paper, plus a point, while the bank and the households hold all of it — walked up by the market's read of the city's books, so a dial at 3% and a debt-free treasury with a bank whose money costs it nothing is a city paying 3%. Until 0.7.7 the bank's strain added up to eighteen points on top of that, and it is gone ([the bank](#13-the-bank)). Since 0.7.15 the floor is split by who holds the paper, Jerus's reading of the backstop: *"if bank is in a pickle, and central bank is at 100% then your debt isnt priced at tge bank, ira proportional"*. Until 0.7.0 it was the dial less a two-point discount, a named constant its own comment called the one number in the file that did not describe anything real; with it went a city borrowing below its own central bank's rate.

```
floor = max(MIN_RATE, policy + (1 − s) × max(0, the bank's cost of funds + MIN_MARGIN − policy))
// s: the central bank's share of all the city's paper, notes included, because the bank holds the notes
```

At s = 0 that is the floor 0.7.14 had, to the bit; at s = 1 the bank's state no longer touches the city's rate. Because the bank's money costs it almost nothing when it is flush, the floor is often the bank's point rather than the dial: on the default seed on 28 September the dial ended at 0.01% and the floor at 1.00%.

Two independent measures move the rest — debt against annual GDP, and debt against annual tax revenue — each a linear ramp to five points of spread and then flat. The city's own overdraft counts as principal, because a city over a million in the red with no bonds was being quoted the floor, and since 0.7.0 so does what it owes its central bank in advances. The cheapest money the market will ever offer is 0.5%. Because face depends on rate and rate depends on face, every quote walks that fixed point six times. The quote *is* the arithmetic: what the screen shows is what gets booked, down to the rate before and after and the points the ask itself cost. A letter grade — AAA to CCC — reports the city's position within the market's own band rather than against typed-in thresholds. Since 0.7.14 a reloaded city's rate is the live city's to the bit: the debt market strikes it from four inputs, and one of them, the overdraft, used to be struck again on load from cash that had moved after the month's strike, up to a basis point away, so the save carries the four and the rate.

**The curve.** Jerus: *"the short term rates, aka the one you choose, those should be basically the tbill rate, the others change just as in real life."* Since 0.7.1 every price of the city's own paper — the quote, the issue, the buyback, the market value and the borrow page, which lists the curve one row per maturity — is read off one function at the paper's maturity, `DebtManager.priceAt(debt, months)`:

```
rate(months) = floor + credit spread + termPremium(months) − compression(months)
termPremium  nothing to a year · linear to the ten-year entry · linear between entries · flat past fifty years
compression  what the central bank's holdings take off it — see the central bank
```

*The term premium, in points over the dial — DebtManager.TERM_PREMIUM_10Y … 50Y, provisional, Jerus's numbers to settle*

| Maturity | 10 yr | 20 yr | 30 yr | 40 yr | 50 yr |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Premium | 0.50 | 0.90 | 1.15 | 1.35 | 1.50 |

A note carries no premium, so the short end is the floor and `getRate()` — what every screen means by the city's rate, the strip's *city* line and the year book's `interestRate` — stays exactly that; a five-year serial carries 48/108 of the ten-year entry. The credit spread is the same at every maturity, so a hike moves the whole curve in parallel and a city that over-borrows pays more at every point of it, and paper already on the books keeps its coupon and its months, so locking in fifty-year money before a hike is a real decision. **Term loans are issued only at ten, twenty, thirty, forty or fifty years** (`LongTermBond.MATURITIES`), at home and in dollars: any other term is refused in words — *"Term loans are issued at 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 years."* — and the Finances chips step by ten. Issue and buyback read the same function, so `RestructureCheck`'s round trip is still neutral by construction, and `CreditCheck`'s section 11 walks the rest: a debt-free note at exactly the dial, each maturity the dial plus its entry, the interpolation, a hike and a debt both parallel, a 25-year request refused and booking nothing, and a twenty-year bond bought back the same month for what it raised, bar the issuance cost.

**Issuance costs** \$12k fixed plus a 0.75% underwriting spread, taken off the proceeds and never rolled into the face — otherwise the bond would be worth more than it raised the instant it was signed. **Buyback** pays cash only and refuses to overdraw, because borrowing at the market rate to retire cheaper paper is strictly worse; since 0.7.1 it pays at the curve's rate for the months the bond has left, and it pays every holder its share, where until 0.7.0 it paid nobody at all and a dollar bond's price left the treasury for nowhere on the books. A city that runs out of cash no longer sells its bank an emergency note; since 0.7.0 its central bank advances the gap, up to a ceiling the player sets ([the central bank](#14-the-central-bank)). **When the treasury cannot pay for an order**, the Build screen offers two things: since 0.7.10 first a twenty-year bond (`Game.BUILD_BOND_YEARS`) whose face is solved so that the cash it brings covers the gap (`Game.quoteLongBondForCash()`), because a building outlives either loan, and then the six-month note it always offered (`Game.BUILD_NOTE_MONTHS`), each with its rate, face, cash, monthly cost, cost in all and what happens at the end. In a probe on 0.7.10, a Standard city buying its water plant on the note alone went D\$16.2M overdrawn when the note fell due, and on the sized bond never went below D\$0.53M and never drew an advance; `NewGameCheck`'s section 11 asserts the sizing at every maturity.

### Who holds the paper

Jerus: *"yes households should be able to hold."* Since 0.7.1 every domestic bond says who holds it — the principal held by the households and by the central bank, the bank whatever is left — and the split is what makes a bond market rather than a loan. At the settle after an issue the households go first, a fifth of it for every point it yields over the deposit rate and never more than half, out of savings past the cushion; the bank buys the rest and is the residual buyer; the central bank never buys at issue, because buying from its own treasury is printing, which is the advances' line — bar one exception since 0.7.15, the par of its own maturing paper, which it takes again at issue as an add-on ([the central bank](#14-the-central-bank)). Coupons and principal are split by the shares struck before the payment: the bank's the way they always went, the households' into savings as untaxed investment income, the central bank's destroyed and remitted. A household short of money sells its paper back to the bank's desk at the month's market value before its dollars and its shares, and a leaver sells on the way out; since 0.7.15 a central bank buying past what the bank holds takes the households' paper by the same door. Sent home by the playtest's `-Dplaytest.borrowAtHome`, the households took 38% of each issue at the settle and one at the cap of half, were paid $6–92M of coupons over a run and sold back in 15 to 239 months, every sale a household short of cash (0.7.1). `HoldersCheck` proves each of those, and fails with a residual if the dollar buyback's audit line is deleted; its ninth section has the central bank at the whole of the paper buying the households' once the bank's is gone.

**The discount accretes.** A term bond's discount — face less what it raised — used to be booked as one month's interest at the settle: $60M of it in one month on seed 0 sent home, taxed, and 45% of it payable to savers. Since 0.7.1 each bond carries its own `discountLeft` and earns it straight-line over its life, the bank earning its share a month at a time and carrying what it has not yet earned against its book (`Bank.unearnedDiscount`), so its equity does not move at the settle.

**The bank never paid for the city's paper**, from at least 0.4.3 until 0.6.11. Every bond and bill the city sells is sold between two presses, and the month snapshotted what the bank owed for it *after* the top-of-tick clear, so `bank.lend()` was handed zero for every domestic issue: the paper went onto the bank's book at face, the coupons and the principal came in, and the cash never went out — equity from nothing on one side, the treasury's money from nowhere on the other. The snapshot is taken before the clear now, and what the bank still owes is carried against its pool in the audit and saved, so a city saved between the issue and the settle still pays. A section of `BankCheck` causes it — $31,000k of paper sold for $30,490.55k, the bank's cash moving by exactly the ordinary month plus that — and fails four ways on the old order. No seed moved, because the playtest's advisor only ever borrowed the cheaper dollars. What the fix uncovered is why the central bank exists: held at a 10% dial, six seeds' treasuries ran dry, and the emergency notes they had lived on free priced at 27–36% once the bank really paid for them and compounded to $193 quadrillion on seed 0 and NaN on seed 6. *A free number had been holding a floor.*

### Rolling what falls due

Jerus: *"the game checks whats going to mature next month, and issues what the treasury is lacking … this doesnt take care of the treasury short of cash, thats the central bank thing"*. Since 0.7.13 the treasury has a setting on both borrow pages with three positions — **by hand**, **same structure** and **12-month notes** — and a new game founds on *same structure*; an older save and the bare city the harnesses and the playtest use keep it by hand. `Rollover` runs at the top of the month, in the gap between presses where a player's own issue lands:

- **What falls due** is the principal due next month, piece by piece, at home and abroad, off each instrument's own schedule.
- **Last year's surplus nets it first** (Jerus: *"Net of last year's surplus"*): the last twelve months' budget surplus that no earlier roll has used, capped at the treasury's cash and at what falls due. A deficit year nets nothing, and a ledger makes each year's surplus net once — shared since 0.7.14 with the city's fund, which takes its December share first. Since 0.7.15 the surplus pays the market's part of what falls due before the central bank's par (Jerus: *"Surplus pays everyone"*), so a city in surplus clears its paper whoever holds it.
- **The rest is issued pro rata, sized to raise the cash it needs** (Jerus: *"Enough to raise the cash"*). In the same structure each piece rolls into its own instrument, term and currency — dollars into dollars abroad, or at home when the window is shut, and a serial's instalment into a new serial of its original term; on 12-month notes everything rolls into a local twelve-month note. Below the smallest issue the model makes nothing is issued and the maturity is paid from cash.
- **A month early**, because the proceeds wait a month in the treasury: pre-funding, which Canada's own rule asks for — liquidity for at least a month of net projected cash flows, refinancing included.

It does not cover a treasury short for its spending; the central bank's advances still do that. And **rolling for cash capitalises interest**: paper sells under its face, so an issue sized to raise the maturity's cash has a larger face than the paper it repays, and the old paper's interest is borrowed into the new principal at every roll. Face for face was measured and Jerus chose cash. The default and autopilot runs were line for line 0.7.12's, because their cities owe nothing at a maturity or net it whole; on a Lean founding seven seeds of eight rolled and repaid, $1.68B of face for $1.26B, and seed 0 spiralled — its twenty-year paper raised 0.34 to 0.59 of its face as the rate climbed to 26.8%, each roll was 1.7 to 2.9 times the face of the last, and it ended owing $476.6T with the central bank owed $370.7T and 2,423 people (0.7.13).

> **Nothing limits the paper at home**
>
> The price of the city's paper stops at the dial plus ten points of spread and the term premium; the bank buys whatever the households leave, funded at a window with no cap; debt service is a promise, paid past the advances ceiling; and only abroad does a window shut. Lean seed 0's $476.6T was that, and so are the spirals of 0.7.14 and 0.7.15 — a held 25% city borrowing from its bank to buy the bank's preferred, and five of eight Insane cities. The holdings dial at 100% makes the central bank the buyer when nobody else is; it does not limit what the city can sell. A market limit — a buyer's refusal, or a debt-service rule at home — is on the list, and Jerus's to design.

### Borrowing in somebody else's money

USD versions of all three instruments, **treasury only**. A foreign bond holds its face and coupon in dollars; every public getter answers in local money at today's rate, so a devaluation makes the debt dearer everywhere in the game at once without a call site knowing. Priced on *exports*, not GDP — the only dollars a city has ever earned came from selling something abroad: a 2% world base, deliberately below the domestic floor (that is the trap), plus a solvency term on dollar debt as years of exports and a service term on next year's bill, capped at 16%. Because the measure is taken in local money, a devaluation worsens the ratio, raises the premium, and makes the next bond dearer — Mexico 1994 and Argentina 2001 without a special case.

**The world's paper has a curve** since 0.7.2: `foreignCurveRate(months)` is the world's base plus the country premium plus the same term-premium table, so a dollar issue prices by maturity and a dollar bond is valued at its remaining months on it — the dial moving no longer moves a dollar bond's value, and the country premium moving does. On the way the dollar quote was found to be a **money pump**: it scaled the service the city already owed and left the new bond's own out, so a thirty-year dollar round trip netted the city $7.5M over eight rounds. It prices its own coupons into the premium now, by a fixed point (`quoteForeignRate(Debt, months)`, walked by `Game.selfPricedForeignRate()`), and `RestructureCheck`'s dollar round trip, which fails on 0.7.1, is neutral by construction. A dollar bond bought back is declared leaving the country.

The **window shuts** on conditions the player can see coming: 14 years of exports owed, service past 45% of exports, dollars owed and nothing sold abroad, or five years after a default. Existing paper still falls due. At issue the player chooses to convert and spend or to hold the dollars as reserves. **Default** tears every foreign bond off the books, no cash moves, the ratios read as perfect — and nobody lends a defaulter a dollar for five years, with a scar on the price that outlasts the closed window. It also fires on its own when the treasury goes a full year of tax revenue into the red with dollars falling due — and since the central bank advances every shortfall at the top of the month, only on a month whose own bills, a balloon falling due, come to more than a year of revenue; whether the rule should read the advances is on the list.

Since 0.7.13 the land office borrows dollars too: a plot paid for out of the vault that the vault cannot cover opens a funding page offering a twenty-year dollar bond or a six-month dollar note sized to the dollar gap (`quoteForeignForCash()`), whose dollars are held in the vault and the plot bought from them ([land](#17-land)); a young city's first dollar loan for land can shut the window for its next one, by the rule that shuts it on dollars owed with nothing sold abroad. And since 0.7.14 an Insane city is founded owing a twenty-year dollar bond at 3% for the ground it starts on ([founding a city](#16-founding-a-city)).

## 13. The bank

*Every loan in the city is the Commercial Bank's money, and since 0.7.7 the bank is run as a business: it prices a loan from what the loan costs it, chooses what it pays its savers, holds a capital target of its own and pays its owners what it does not need. Since 0.7.8 a sector defaults a slice at a time, since 0.7.11 the landlords borrow on insured mortgages, since 0.7.12 a firm that cannot pay ends the way a firm does, and since 0.7.14 a bank that fails passes to the city.*

> **What was asked for**
>
> Jerus: *"lets make banks realistic, and remember, its a business, it wants to make money."* The reading of his 0.7.5 city that came before it found the bank deepening both of that city's crises without starting either: a strained bank added up to eighteen points to every rate in the city, which caused the defaults, the write-offs and the lost equity that strained it further. The plan was three batches — the price, the capital, the tab — anchored on the figures of Canada's big banks, and 0.7.7 to 0.7.9 built them. Of its capital he said *"the bank chooses."*

### The bank is somebody

Every loan in the city — to a sector, to a household, and whatever of the city's own paper the households and the central bank do not hold — is the **Commercial Bank's** money: one building, **29 jobs** a branch, its own tab, and a trading desk that trades on the exchange's books like anybody else; since 0.7.12 it also underwrites every business's bonds, and holds them when it chooses to. Its capacity is the tighter of two limits, what its capital allows and six times the savings its branches can reach, 250,000 a branch, and how much of that its book uses is its strain. Past it the bank does not refuse, and whatever it lends that its own money and the savings it reaches do not fund it borrows at the central bank's window — abroad, until 0.7.0 — and what that money costs goes into the price of whatever it lends, where until 0.7.7 its strain added a premium ramping to **18 points** on every rate in the city. A city with no bank is simply a bank with no capacity, and since 0.7.7 it is priced the way any loan is, with the window's money as its funding: Jerus's decision was that a city with no bank yet pays *"normal"* prices, not a punitive one. Branches build themselves through the retail advisor when strain passes 70% — never, since 0.7.11, while the bank is under its minimum — and a branch whose book has not kept its staff for two years closes, one a month and never the last.

**The bank lends to households**, for cars and for a short month, and the audit already carried both legs of that: the cash leaving the bank and the debt arriving on the household balance each other with nothing new written. A write-off costs the book, not the cash.

### Nothing borrows below what the money costs

For most of the project the bank could be made to lend at a rate below what it was paying for the funds. Three separate mechanisms did it — the city's bond floor, the business desk's spread over a risk-free rate, and a carry trade that borrowed abroad to buy domestic paper — and none of them was wrong on its own terms. The bank simply had no veto.

```
cost of funds = depositRate × (1 − wholesaleShare) + windowRate × wholesaleShare     // the window: the dial and a quarter point since 0.7.7, a point from 0.7.0
any rate      = max(riskFree, costOfFunds + MIN_MARGIN) + its own premium   // MIN_MARGIN = .01, one point; every rate until 0.7.7, the city's paper since
```

One rule, three call sites until 0.7.7, and the city's paper alone since. It is **blended, not marginal** — the first cut used whichever source the last dollar came from, and the floor flipped between 1.9% and 13.6% across twelve consecutive months. And it is **struck once, at the close of the month, and carried in the save**: the live path priced mid-month and the load path priced at the end, so a city reloaded from disk quoted a different rate than the one it had just been running at — 0.0135 against 0.0133, which is the kind of divergence a harness catches and a player never would.

> **Sixteen seeds, before and after**
>
> Bank failures **5.0 → 0.0** median. Recapitalisation **\$3.8bn → \$0**. Closing equity **\$6.6bn → \$9.1bn**. Wholesale funding **24–47% → 0–8%** of income. Months run at a loss **44–58% → 3–14%**. Every seed lifetime-profitable, and the "gentler financing" calibration was not touched to get it.

The obvious next step — make the bank a real intermediary, funding domestic investment out of domestic savings — was measured and abandoned. **The bank lends 1.87% of its deposits at home and runs at 31–49% of the capacity it already has.** The city's savings are on the order of two hundred thousand times what its productive sector wants to borrow. The bank is demand-limited, not funding-limited, and no amount of deposit-gathering changes that. On the default seed on 28 September it ended with $293bn deposited and $131M lent, 13% of its capacity.

### What a loan costs

Since 0.7.7 a loan is priced the way a bank prices one, as the sum of four costs (`Bank`, WHAT A LOAN COSTS): the **funds-transfer price**, what the next dollar costs it for the loan's term — the policy rate while it holds spare reserves, which would otherwise earn the dial at the central bank, the window's rate while it borrows there, blended by how it is funded, and the curve's term premium for the maturity; the **running costs**, a trailing year of payroll and upkeep over the larger of its book and what its capital could carry, so a young bank is not charged its whole payroll on an empty book; the **expected loss** of a sound book through the cycle, `BASE_LOSS_RATE` 0.4%, about what Canada's big banks provision in a normal year; and the **capital charge**, the equity the loan ties up at the return the market prices the bank's shares on — 12.5% at the defaults, the world's rate and the three-point premium over the 40% payout (`Equity.requiredYield()`) — over what that money would cost as debt. **Prime** is the four for a sound business borrowing for thirty-six months. The carry trade pays the three without the loss; a household pays the four at its own weight plus its spread for the months of income it owes; a business's own risk and a landlord's insured mortgage are below.

```
prime = funds-transfer price + running costs + expected loss + capital charge
// the default seed's last month on 28 September: 0.12 + 1.06 + 0.40 + 2.04 = 3.62% on a dial of 0.01%
```

The expected loss is a constant because the bank's own record, tried twice, was a disaster twice: a whole sector was one borrower in the model then, so the record was lumpy by construction, and a five-year window priced prime at 77.9% in month 12 of seed 0. In calm years on 0.7.7's eight seeds prime ran 1.7 to 2.0 points over the dial, where Canada's runs 2.2; the cities grew more slowly in their first century and ended about 9% smaller, and the bank failed 4 times against 19.

### What savers get, and the fees

Since 0.7.7 the bank chooses what it pays its savers — Jerus: *"it can pass on less or more if it wants"* — and it chooses by how it is funded: 0.35 of the dial when it is flush with reserves, because its next deposit would only earn the dial at the central bank less the cost of the account, rising toward 0.90 while it borrows at the window, because every deposit it finds saves it the window's rate, and moving a sixth of the way a month, so most of a move reaches savers inside a year and none of it in one step. It never pays them more than the smaller of what its interest margin leaves after payroll and upkeep and the savers' own share of that margin. The second bound was the gate's catch: the bank counts the city's savings as deposits without holding them, the one stated simplification in its header, and held at 10% the first finished build paid its savers every dollar it earned on them and failed 184 times against 0.7.6's 78. Over the eight seeds savers got 0.37 to 0.44 of the dial on average, where real banks pass on about 0.4. On the default seed on 28 September the bank passed on 0.29 of it on average, its margin holding its savers under the rate it chose in 3,157 months of the run.

It replaced two rules that are history now. From the bank's founding it paid savers 45% of what it earned in interest (`DEPOSIT_PASS_THROUGH`), and bid higher only when it was short of deposits; and since 0.7.3 it quoted no more than it charged, because a founding bank's first month paid savers 45% of everything it earned, the placement of its own capital included, over $5.7k of deposits, which read as 7,567% a year and would have put the households' spending at its floor in month 3 of every seed. That cap bound in 17 to 236 months of each default run. Both went with 0.7.7.

**Fees**, since 0.7.7: every housed household pays an account fee of $12 a month at founding prices, indexed to the cost of living, on its own line of the household books and declared to the audit, and orphans, prisoners and the unhoused pay nothing; and new lending pays 1%, out of a business loan's proceeds, grossed up so that the firm still covers its shortfall, and added to a household's or a car's loan. On 0.7.7's seeds the running costs were 0–7% of the bank's revenue against a real bank's 49–60%, and fees 0–6% against about 39%, because its payroll is tiny against what it lends; that was left as measured.

### Its capital, and what it does with its profit

Since 0.7.8 the bank keeps its capital as a business does:

- **A loss allowance** in IFRS 9's two stages: a year's expected loss on a sound borrower and the lifetime loss on one in trouble — a sector's firms past 0.9 of their assets, a family past half its credit ceiling — with write-offs drawn against it first and the provision the month's move in it. Its loans sit on its balance sheet net of it.
- **Its own capital target**: the 8% minimum plus the larger of Basel's 2.5-point conservation buffer and the worst year of provisions it has lived through, capped at the whole Basel stack of 8.5 points (`MAX_BUFFER`) — uncapped, one restructure put the target at 48–108% and stalled a city at 8,348 people. A young bank aims at 10.5% and one that has lived through a crisis at up to 16.5%, and the top of its band is 2.5 points over that.
- **A payout rule**: nothing under its target, 45% of its profit after tax inside its band (RBC paid 43%), and past the top of the band the excess as well, a twelfth a month. 0.7.7's bank paid out almost nothing, because its dividend was capped at its cash, and sat on $26.6–50.5bn of equity against a book of $1.7–10bn.
- **Lending that tightens with its capital**: free at or over its target; between the minimum and the target a borrower's debt may grow at most 1% × x/(1 − x) a month, where x is how far its capital stands from the minimum to the target — nothing at the minimum, 1% halfway; under the minimum only what keeps its borrowers going, a business's interest reserve and a family's month of interest. The families' credit reads the bank's state for the first time.
- **Its own shares** issued only under its target and bought back only with capital over it, and booked as capital, not as trading income — 0.7.7 had booked $8.2bn of them as $8.65bn of desk profit on seed 0 — and its desk buys other companies' shares only while the bank would still hold its target with them on its books at the weight Basel gives a trading book.
- **A leverage ratio** since 0.7.11: equity of at least 3% of everything it has lent, whatever that weighs (`LEVERAGE_RATIO_MIN`, Basel III's), which floors every requirement above — the minimum, the target, the payout, the two spare-capital limits and the lending rule. It came with the insured mortgages, which weigh nothing: without it the bank paid out the equity they never asked of it, grew thin and fell back into its old branch trap, and with it and two other fixes the failures with no loan loss went from 72 to none.

On 0.7.8's eight seeds, in its growth years, the bank held 19.2% against a 16.5% target, earned 13.0% on its equity (RBC 16.3%), paid out 76% of its profit and provisioned 0.41% of its loans a year (RBC 0.43%), and its worst year was 38–109% of its weighted book, so its target sat at `MAX_BUFFER` in every seed. On the default seed on 28 September, over its 216 growth years of 333, the median year held 63% against a target of 15.5%, earned 6.1% on its equity and paid out 82% of its profit.

### Business credit

A separate hierarchy, because a business loan must never charge the city's cash. Interest reaches the treasury only through the sector's income statement. Loans are interest-only bullets over 36 months, fixed for all of them at the rate they were written at, originated automatically to cover a hole and, since 0.7.8's pricing, for buildings too; a landlord's homes are on mortgages instead. Until 0.7.7 rates ran the city's rate + 1% to 8% on debt-to-assets, the base never under the bank's cost of funds plus a point, plus a point for each prior write-down up to three — on the default seed on 22 September, with the city's note at 1.00%, the spotless sectors with little debt borrowed at 2.00%, a leveraged landlord with no write-down at 7.40%, and a sector with three or more write-downs at 5.00%. Since 0.7.7 they sit on prime, and since 0.7.8 on the default curve below.

**The underwriter leaves a gap.** It will lend to 0.9× assets; the default point is 1.5×. They used to be the same number, so the desk parked every borrower exactly on the write-down line. Until 0.7.8 a sector past 1.5× was written down whole to 0.6× and blocked from borrowing — twelve months the first time, twenty-four the second, thirty-six after that, a ban that also stops its investment advisor expanding on credit — and over 4,000 months that pair of changes took write-offs from $25.8bn to $1.35bn. Since 0.7.8 only a sector with nothing left is written down whole, and the rest of its trouble is a slice at a time.

**There was no concentration limit**, and a fixture found the hole by accident on 17 September: Materials built its first plant, had to buy a fleet of lorries as well as the plant, borrowed $57,939 from a bank with $50,292 of equity — thirty-eight per cent of the whole book in one name — and defaulted in month 70, taking the bank's equity to minus $2,628. Neither half is a bug in the bank: a sector that buys vehicles as well as machines is a riskier borrower, which is the mechanic. And 0.7.2 found the hole again from the other side: on the new path Manufacturing borrowed $74M against a bank whose equity was $30M, for a Fabrication Works that loses money before interest, and was written off at month 166 and its restructured remainder at 178 in four seeds of the eight — all of the rise in the ensemble's bank failures, 8 to 19. From 0.7.8 on, one sector holding 30–73% of the book was under every failure the bank had, and 0.7.12 answered it with a price rather than a limit (below).

### A sector is many firms

As 0.7.8 was first built, the bank failed 92 times on the default eight against 0.7.7's 4, and the trace said why: a whole sector was one borrower, and when Real Estate or Manufacturing restructured, the bank lost 60% of everything that sector owed in a single month, 37–185% of its weighted book in its worst year. Jerus was offered three ways on and chose the third, *"go for option C"*: a sector stands for many firms, and only its weakest part goes bust, a slice at a time. How many is Merton's structural model, the basis of Moody's KMV:

```
PD(L) = N( ln(L / 1.5) / σ )         // a year; L the sector's debt over its assets, 1.5 INSOLVENCY_TRIGGER
h     = 1 − (1 − PD)^1/12            // the month's share of its debt whose firms default
σ     = ASSET_VOLATILITY 0.25      // the one new number, Jerus's to settle; the literature puts it at 20–35%
```

So 1.5 is where a *firm* defaults. The sector's own books carry the common shock and σ is the spread of fortunes among its firms, which averages out over many of them, so the flow is deterministic. Each month the defaulting share of its debt is written off pro rata across its loans and bonds at each instrument's own loss, and the firms keep their plant; its leverage falls, so next month's hazard is smaller. Only a sector with nothing left, or one still past the line that nobody will lend to after a write-down, is written down whole by the old rule, and only that **backstop** goes on its record, with the surcharge and the ban. The allowance reads the same curve, staged firm by firm. **A loan is priced by it**: prime, plus a loan's loss given default times PD(L) less what prime already carries, plus a point for each write-down on its record up to three, plus since 0.7.12 the capital its book's concentration asks of it — at the leverage the loan would leave the borrower at, a project's building counted, and read on the borrower's last quarter (`STATEMENT_MONTHS` 3), as a bank reads statements, while the defaults read the month, because firms fail on what they actually owe. A sound borrower pays prime, one at the watch line 0.11 points over it, one at 1.2 times its assets 4.25 and one at the default point 12.1.

It took four attempts to stand up. Pricing by the curve cut lending past 1.0 by two thirds; Basel's large-exposure rule, with the rest of a big loan syndicated to banks abroad on Jerus's choice, sent 99% of business lending abroad, ran prices to 3.9 times founding and still failed the bank 101 times, and was deleted, because a sector is many firms and Basel's rule is for one firm or a group tied by control, not an industry; reading a borrower on its quarter was the best single fix of the four. It shipped at 39 failures, and under every one of them one sector held 30–73% of the book. A failing sector's buildings are sold to the builders for their material ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)).

### How a firm that cannot pay ends

0.7.12 put a bond beside the loan ([the owners, the bonds and the exchange](#9-the-owners-the-bonds--the-exchange)) and found, partway through, Luxury Retail's late collapses running on an interest-free overdraft: a till allowed below zero, owing nobody, for hundreds of months. Everything after that was about how a firm that cannot pay ends, and each answer is a real rule that Jerus chose:

- **Can't pay means default**: beside the balance-sheet test the model had, the cash-flow test of Canada's *Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act*, s. 2. A short month recalls its dollars abroad, sells the other sectors' bonds it holds and borrows, and what it still cannot pay defaults a slice the size of the part it cannot pay.
- **Credit lines stay open**: the capital rule rations growth — project loans and new mortgages — and working capital, a short month's cover, the interest reserve and a rollover, is honoured up to the 0.9 ceiling and the default point, as banks did in 2008 and in March 2020. The first cut treated a short month's cover as growth and set off a credit crunch.
- **Interim financing**: after the write-down, what is still unpaid is lent as a loan that ranks ahead of all other debt (`InterimLoan`; Canada's CCAA s. 11.2, and §364 in the United States), and nothing is forgiven on that path; a sector still past the line after the write-down finds nobody to lend and goes to the backstop, and a ban stops growth lending, not what keeps a firm running.
- **Nothing past the default point**: no door lends to a sector whose leverage, read on the quarter, is past 1.5.

**Concentration is priced, not capped**, which was Jerus's choice. The bank holds Basel's IRB capital against each sector's loans, with a correlation that rises with how concentrated its book is across sectors, allocated to each sector by the Euler rule and so into its loan rate; the single-industry multiplier is Basel III's 1.25, set for large financial institutions and kept and flagged. And since 0.7.12 each instrument recovers what it recovers in the world: 75% of a bank loan and 45% of a bond. Against 0.7.11 on eight seeds, failures went 115 → 1 in the default setup and 265 → 9 on autopilot, the money the city put into its bank $134.7B → $3.1B and $228.8B → $2.0B, and the money created by forgiven overdrafts fell from $19.9B partway through the batch to $0.095B, all of it the backstop's. What still failed the bank was the young one on its $32M of founding capital, before month 1,000, when Manufacturing or Automotive went. On the default seed on 28 September 1,535 sector-months defaulted for want of cash over the run, 1,276 of them shells — sectors holding no plant that still owed something — which nothing winds up.

### The landlords take a mortgage

A trace of 0.7.10 found what had stopped the cranes. The landlords financed fifty-year buildings on three-year interest-only bullets: on autopilot seed 0, months 2,280 to 2,490, their maturing loans went unrolled, the till fell to minus $6.8B, every new building had to borrow that hole on top of its cost, and nothing was built for about 200 months with homes 37% short. Held at 10%, the test asked gross rent to cover 1.25 times the interest on the whole cost, about 14.5% a year, where a home earned 8–9%. Jerus chose *"Mortgages"*, on *"CMHC (Canada)"*'s rulebook, and *"Insured by the city"*. Since 0.7.11 a landlord's residential building is bought with at least 15% of its own funds and a **mortgage** for the rest (`Mortgage`): at most 85% of the cost, a level payment over 40 years at a rate fixed for 10 and renewed at the day's rate, and the lender's test is the building's net operating income — rent less maintenance and property tax — at least 1.20× the payment. The city insures it: the landlord pays CMHC's premium, 5.00% of the loan and 0.75% more for forty years, added to the loan and paid to the treasury as revenue, and when a landlord is written down the treasury pays the bank what came off insured balances, as a promise. The bank weighs an insured mortgage at nothing and sets nothing aside for it, and prices it at its ten-year funds-transfer price and its running costs, with no expected loss, plus the capital the leverage ratio ties up, 0.41 to 0.64 points at the defaults. Everything else keeps its thirty-six-month loan and its 1.25 interest test.

The stall went: through seed 0's old window homes rose from 35,141 to 36,464 and the till stayed at or above zero. The 10% city stayed small, which is the honest answer at a 10% real rate: the 1.20 test on a forty-year paydown asks net rent of 12.2% of the cost a year. The insurance took in $3.9B of premiums over the eight default seeds against $2.1M of claims, and held at 10% it lost money for the first time, $404M of claims against $56M of premiums. And the bank failed more, 115 times against 42: without the landlords' $6B of fully weighted bullets it was small, $161M of equity at month 2,400 against $1.13B, and the industrial sector that failed it owed five to six times its equity. Jerus shipped it with that open, and the next batch was the bonds. On the default seed on 28 September the landlords wrote 293 mortgages over the run and renewed 879, and the insurance took $185M of premiums against $70k of claims.

### When the bank fails

A bank that has lost more than it owns has **failed**, which is one of the shocks that can start a run on the currency. The path from 278 jobs a branch to 29, a deposit limit from $60k to $250k, honest underwriting and an escalating exclusion once took it from **308 failures in 4,000 months to none in seven seeds of eight**; what each batch since has done to that count is in the table below. Until 0.7.14 the city could put capital into a failed bank and got nothing for it, and the hole was declared to the audit as absorbed from outside the city. Jerus, on the owners of a failed bank: *"City takes the shares … but later bank can dilute by issuing shares... we dont want commercial to be owned by government fully in the long run"*. Since 0.7.14 the treasury has a setting, *When the bank fails*: Automatic, which new games found on, or Wait for my button, which older saves and the harnesses' bare city keep. Either way the resolution (`Game.resolveBank()`) is the same:

- every common share passes to the city's rescue book, the households', the world's and the desk's alike, and the old owners get nothing, as under the bail-in regime of Canada's deposit insurer and as with Northern Rock in 2008;
- the city's preferred and its warrants are cancelled, because the hole took them;
- the city pays the hole and the capital to reopen at one and a half times the minimum, as a promise: the treasury's cash first, and the central bank advances the rest at the next settle, past the ceiling if it must (Jerus: *"Central bank advances it"*);
- and the bank reopens the same month.

Nothing enters from outside the city any more; a bank waiting for the button carries its hole at the window. The city's stake falls only as the bank sells new shares (Jerus: *"New issues only"*), which it does when it is under its target and when it repays the preferred: on 0.7.14's default runs the median stake was 72.8% five years after a resolution, 51.0% at ten and 58.8% at twenty-five, and the player can sell the rescue book by hand.

**A standing bank under its minimum asks for preferred shares.** Jerus wanted *"a popup message saying bank wants to issue you shares or something"*, and since 0.7.14 the inbox carries the bank's offer, on the terms of the United States' 2008 Capital Purchase Program: enough to take it back to its target, but at least 1% and at most 3% of its risk-weighted assets; a cumulative dividend of 5% a year, 9% from the fifth anniversary, paid only out of equity over its target, and no common dividend while any is unpaid; for three years no buybacks and no rise in the common dividend; and warrants on common shares worth 15% of the amount, for ten years. The player accepts or declines, and the bank asks again a quarter later either way (Jerus: *"Quarter"*); a treasury short of the money is shown the build screen's two funding offers. Each block is repaid at its third anniversary at par with its unpaid dividends, from the bank's capital over its target and the rest by new common sold to the public (Jerus: *"Sell new shares to repay"*), which dilutes the city's own common, and after the last block the warrants are bought back at fair value. The balance sheet has a third equity line for it, *Preferred shares (the city)*.

On 0.7.14's default runs the city bought 45 blocks for $1.26B and was repaid $1.22B at three years, $996M of it by new shares, with nothing outstanding at the end. Held at 25% the preferred is circular capital: the city borrows from the bank to buy the bank's preferred, every offer is larger than the last, and the eight seeds bought $962T of it with the advances peaking at $20.4 quadrillion; Jerus kept it, *"Keep as built"*, and the limit on the city's own paper would close it. On the default seed on 28 September the bank failed once, in month 442: the city paid $40.9M to resolve it, all of it from its cash, the old owners lost $45.6M at the last price, and the city still held 4.2% of the bank at the end; six preferred offers were accepted for $234M, and none was outstanding at the end.

*Bank failures over eight seeds, as each batch measured them against the build before it — a last-bit rounding difference moves a count by about three (0.7.8)*

| Batch | Default | Autopilot | Held at 10% |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0.7.7, the price | 19 → 4 | 13 → 1 | 78 → 40 |
| 0.7.8, the capital and the slices | 4 → 39 | 1 → 49 | 40 → 284 |
| 0.7.10, the smaller founding | 39 → 42 | 49 → 76 | — |
| 0.7.11, the mortgages | 42 → 115 | 76 → 265 | 234 → 213 |
| 0.7.12, the bonds | 115 → 1 | 265 → 9 | 213 → 77 |
| 0.7.14, the city takes the shares | 1 → 6 | 9 → 17 | 71 → 104 |

0.7.14's runs part from 0.7.13's only at the first month the city puts capital into its bank, where Jerus's rules replace the old playtest's gift: its player had put up to a quarter of the treasury into any bank under its minimum, every month, for nothing. 0.7.15's default and autopilot runs are 0.7.14's to the byte.

### The Bank tab

Jerus: *"a redesign of the bank UI info, cause when you click on bank you dont even see all the relevant stuff, lets make banks realistic."* Since 0.7.9 the tab's landing answers whether the bank is healthy, and why, without a click: a status sentence with the figure that decides it (`Bank.status()` — healthy, rebuilding, under its minimum, failed, or no bank); a scorecard of eight — profit this month and over twelve, return on equity against the owners' 12.5%, the capital ratio on a bar against the minimum, its target and the top of its band, credit losses as a share of loans, net interest margin, costs over revenue, what is lent, and deposits; and the **rate ladder**, from the policy rate through what savers get, the funds-transfer price and prime in its parts to a rung for every borrower, every step labelled in points.
