Behind it are six pages — Profit, a Balance sheet since 0.7.13, Lending, Funding, Capital & owners and History — and every figure on them is a model getter, because a dozen on the old tab had been recomputed on the screen and several were wrong: per-branch figures in founding money after a reform, a weight table with no term and no desk that did not foot, *99900.0% capital* with nothing lent, an alert on the wrong line. Since 0.7.11 the capital figures read the leverage ratio when it is the larger requirement and the ladder has an insured rung. The balance sheet sets this month against a year ago, every line opening into its detail, and splits equity into what was paid in and what was retained so that the two add up to it to the cent; deposits are a memo line beside it, because the model does not carry them as the bank's liability. Retained earnings ended below zero in 27 of 0.7.13's 32 runs, because dividends that return excess capital come out of retained while the city's rescues sit in paid-in, and Jerus kept it so. Since 0.7.14 the landing carries the resolution and the preferred offer, and the balance sheet a third equity line. `BankCheck`'s thirteenth section asserts the arithmetic the tab reads; none of it has been seen on a screen.

## 14. The central bank

*Until 0.7.0 the game had a central bank, and it was the rest of the world. The commercial bank placed its spare cash abroad at the world's 2% and funded its shortfalls abroad; the policy dial only floored the lending rate on top, which is why it stopped mattering past 17%; and money was created only from outside — the founding, exports, capital coming in, the bank's wholesale funding — so the price level had nothing at home to answer to. Five batches, 0.6.11 to 0.7.3, brought the marginal role home, and 0.7.15 made it the buyer of last resort for the city's paper. This is what the central bank is, what it holds, what each of its four dials does, and — measured, and said plainly — how little the rate still moves prices.*

> **What was asked for**
>
> Jerus: *"…we implement a central bank, and basically the central bank would buy gbonds or sell gbonds from thin air … the feds sheet would show how much debt it holds, like debt to itself aka money printing, like QE and QT … and that is the M2 supply or what do you think?"* Decided the same night: a floor system, households who can hold the city's paper, and an autopilot beside the dial. Each batch was gated on the whole suite and on the eight seeds, and the design note that set them out is `the-central-bank.md`.

### The books

`CentralBank` is a balance sheet the player reads, on the Money page under Finances. **Assets:** advances to the commercial bank at the window; advances to the treasury, its overdraft, which is what "printed" means on the screens; the city's paper it holds, at face; and the vault, read from `ForeignAccounts` rather than moved there, because the treasury still buys and sells reserves and the currency's code has to see them. **Liabilities:** reserves and currency, which together are **M0**. Currency is zero — nobody in this city holds cash outside the bank — and kept so that the day somebody does it has a line. Its equity is what the two sides leave.

**Money is made and destroyed here and nowhere else.** An advance, interest on reserves and the remittance are money issued; a repayment, the window's interest and the advances' interest are money retired. `MoneyAudit` sees the central bank as a boundary participant, like the world, and declares both under a scope of its own, so the month's issued less retired is the change in M0 to the cent — the difference between money from thin air and a residual. `CentralBankCheck` section 1 walks a month with every kind of flow in it and asserts exactly that. M0 is a ledger of what this bank has made and not taken back, not a reading of the commercial bank's till, because money reaches the pools without passing through a central bank — exports, capital, the founding — and the two could not both hold the identity.

**M2** is what the public holds: the households' deposits, the sectors', the world's, and currency (`Game.getM2()`). It grows when the bank lends reserves on or the treasury spends printed money, not when the central bank buys from the bank. Both are series, with a year of each on the Money page and a column each in the year book. On the default seed on 22 September the run ends with M0 at $2.39B, all of it reserves, M2 at $78.0B, the central bank having made $18.5B and destroyed $16.1B since founding and remitted $486M to the treasury — and its equity at minus $2.39B, a loss carried from paying interest on reserves in money it made, which is exactly what printing to pay interest on reserves looks like. On 0.7.2's eight default seeds it ended below zero in every one, at minus $1.1B to minus $3.3B. On 28 September, with the dial's median at 0.44% over the run, the default seed ended with M0 at $1.48M, M2 at $293.4B, $8.08B made and $8.08B destroyed since founding and $426M remitted, and its equity at $32.1M: the vault it counts as its asset, less $1.48M of loss carried.

### The rate is a floor

The dial is the rate the central bank pays on reserves. The commercial bank's spare cash sits there earning it, where it used to earn the world's 2% abroad, and its shortfalls are borrowed at the **window** at the dial plus `WINDOW_PENALTY` — a quarter point since 0.7.7, the Bank of Canada's own spread, and a point before — where they used to cost the city's own paper rate plus two points and a stretch; a failed bank is charged nothing at the window while it is resolved (0.7.1), because its equity is zero and a charge would fail it again. Savers got their share of what reserves earned — a bank whose only income was its reserves paid them 0.675% at a 3% dial and 2.25% at 10%, the first time the dial had ever reached a household — and since 0.7.7 they get the share of the dial the bank chooses ([the bank](#13-the-bank)). Nothing lends below what reserves earn and nothing borrows above what the window charges, so the dial is the price of money: the city's note prices at its floor plus its spreads, and `MonetaryCheck`'s section 6 reads the city's rate at exactly the dial at 3, 10, 20 and 40% and the bank's lending rate about one to two points over it — 5.02%, 11.28%, 21.02% and 40.98% on 28 September. On the way it found a premium counted twice: the carry trade and the bank's deposit bid were priced off a rate that already carried the strain premium, and `lendingRate()` added it again. The carry trade itself is untouched, and is now the priced alternative rather than the marginal source.

**Interest on reserves is paid in money made for it**, and that is the one place the floor has no floor of its own. Held at 30% or 50% for a whole run, M0 compounds to 10^8 to 3×10^14 $B while prices stay near one — spare cash earning the rate in new money that becomes spare cash — and the same mechanism took M0 to $1.25 quadrillion in the six broke seeds held at 0.7.1's stop of 25%. It is on the list.

**Autopilot.** A toggle on the monetary page hands the dial to the Taylor rule each month — the rule the page already prints, which since 0.7.2 is clamped only by the dial's bound at 100% — until the player's hand takes it back; saved, and held in a playtest by `-Dplaytest.autopilot`; the dial itself is held for a whole run by `-Dplaytest.policyRate`. With the rule on the dial on all eight seeds, 0.7.2 took bank failures from 27 to 17, the dial peaked at 30.5% and no seed spiralled: with the rule's hand on it, a credible real rate holds. Since 0.7.13 a new game founds on the autopilot; an older save keeps the hand it was played with.

**The target is the player's.** Jerus: *"i want to have the dial not target 0 inflation, set it so that you can choose what is your inflation target"*. Since 0.7.4 the rule aims at `inflationTarget`, 2% by default (`DEFAULT_INFLATION_TARGET`, the constant it had been), in half points from nothing to 10%, and since 0.7.15 to 20% — Jerus: *"inflation target can be higher tgan 10%, up yo 20%"* (`MAX_INFLATION_TARGET`). It sits under the autopilot on the monetary page and applies at once, like the ceiling, with chips to 5%, and the rule's sentence is struck live at the target and at another (`ruleRate(inflation, target)`), so that at 5% inflation the page can say the rule sets 7.5% aiming at 2% and 10.5% aiming at nothing without doing the arithmetic itself. It is saved under its own key, an older save reads 2%, and `-Dplaytest.inflationTarget` holds it for a run. The strip's colours read from it ([the currency](#15-prices-the-currency--the-world)).

### Advances, the ceiling, and who is paid

A treasury below zero at the top of the month is advanced its gap at the policy rate, repays from the first cash above zero before anything else, and may owe up to a ceiling in months of its trailing revenue. The emergency note it used to sell its bank is retired, and a save still carrying one runs it off. The ceiling is a dial since 0.7.2 — `advancesCeilingMonths`, 0 to `MAX_ADVANCES_CEILING` 36, default `DEFAULT_ADVANCES_MONTHS` 6, chips at 3, 6, 12, 24 and 36 months on the monetary page — saved under its own key, so an older save reads six, and held in a playtest by `-Dplaytest.advancesMonths`.

Past the ceiling the treasury pays by Jerus's rule, asked what a treasury past its ceiling does: *"pay promises first, cut the rest."* Every payment goes through `Game.treasuryPays(TreasuryLine, amount)`. **Promises** — pensions, EI, health, the schools, the police and prisons, the city's own services, coupons and principal at home and abroad, the interest on the advances, the student loans already lent — are paid whatever it takes, past the ceiling if they must. **Discretionary** lines — the subsidies, the students' grants, repairs to the city's own buildings — are paid only from cash at or above zero once the ceiling has bound, and what they are refused is owed as interest-free **arrears**, by line, listed on the Government tab and paid down first when cash returns. **Purchases** — land, buildings, capital into the bank, reserves, buybacks — are simply not made. The central bank's profit — the interest it takes on its advances and, since 0.7.1, on the paper it holds, less what reserves cost it — is remitted to the treasury the next month as a revenue line; a loss is carried and recovered before anything is remitted again.

It is the floor the overdraft never had. On 0.7.0, held at a 10% dial, the six seeds that had compounded to $193 quadrillion and NaN ended owing $0.1–2.0B, the audit closed every month, and seed 0's bank failures went from 161 to 16; the arrears grew in a straight line rather than compounding, and none of the five that drew recovered. On 0.7.2, with the currency answering the real rate, none of the six draws at all. The default seed on 22 September never drew an advance: it ended owing nothing against a ceiling of $2.71B, six months of its revenue; nor did it on 28 September, against a ceiling of $3.20B.

**Since 0.7.15 a city can run on them from its first month.** Asked whether an Insane city should play before it borrows, Jerus chose *"Play runs on advances"*, and the refusal 0.7.14 had put on the play clock is gone. An Insane city that never borrows pays its land bond's dollar coupon and its founders' pensions in month one from nothing, ends it $6.47k overdrawn, and is advanced the gap at the next settle; its discretionary lines are refused, because a ceiling of no revenue leaves no room, and its private sector pays tax from month two, so a year on its treasury holds $7.1M. The time skip no longer stops at an empty treasury either (*"Skip runs too"*); it says what the central bank advanced. A failed bank's resolution is paid through the same door since 0.7.14, the advances taking whatever the treasury's cash does not ([the bank](#13-the-bank)).

### The holdings dial: QE and QT

Quantity, beside the price. `CentralBank.targetShare` is the share of the city's outstanding *term* paper — serials and term loans, not notes — the central bank aims to hold, from nothing to `MAX_QE_SHARE` — half until 0.7.15, because past half the market it is the market, and all of it since, as a backstop (below); chips every ten points on the monetary page, saved, and held in a playtest by `-Dplaytest.qeShare`. Once a month, in `openMarketOperation()` — after the treasury has settled with its central bank and before the market is priced, so this month's quotes carry it — the holding moves toward the dial by at most `QE_SPEED`, a quarter, of the largest of the dial, the setting before it and the share actually held: four months at most, exactly four to or from nothing, so a sale finishes where a share of the gap never would. It never buys at issue, bar its own maturing par since 0.7.15, and it trades only paper that has already been paid for, pro rata, at the curve's market value — the bank's first, and since 0.7.15 the households' after it; buying is money issued and selling money retired; it carries the paper at face and takes what it paid above or below face into the month's profit, so the remittance carries it. The coupons on its share are destroyed and come back as the remittance: *debt to itself*. The setting before the dial is saved beside it and restored without moving (`restoreTargetShare()`), because the first build forgot the pace on every reload.

```
compression(months) = termPremium(months) × min(1, share of the term paper held / FULL_COMPRESSION_SHARE) × QE_COMPRESSION     // FULL_COMPRESSION_SHARE .5 · QE_COMPRESSION 1.0
```

So at 30% held the fifty-year sits exactly 0.90 points under the table and the note has not moved, and at half the term premium is gone. With the playtest's borrowing sent home and the dial at 30% (0.7.1), the central bank bought exactly 30% of each issue's face in four months from the month after its settle, at 0.99 to 1.05 of face, and took 0.90 points off the fifty-year while it held it. It moved nothing else — the runs match the ones without it month for month until the first purchase and drift apart after, trajectory noise rather than a channel — because the playtest's advisor reads only the short end, which the compression never touches. `CentralBankCheck` sections 11–15 assert the purchase at `QE_SPEED` × 30% at face and at the market value, M0 moved by exactly it, `compression(240)` exact and the note untouched, the coupon destroyed and remitted, the dial to nothing selling back within the speed's months, the pace across a save, and a reform that scales the holdings and not the dial.

**The backstop.** Jerus: *"central bank bond holding can ve 100% if one wants"* — *"for when banks and investors dont want government bonds, its also f bank is in dire state, to not harm it further"*. Since 0.7.15 the dial runs to the whole of the term paper (`MAX_QE_SHARE` 1.0). It buys the bank's paper first and then the households', at the curve's value, through the door a household short of money sells by; the compression stays whole from half, with nothing more past it (`FULL_COMPRESSION_SHARE`); and the city's floor is split by who holds the paper, so that the more of it the central bank holds, the less the bank's state reaches the city's rate ([the city's borrowing](#12-the-citys-borrowing)). And it **rolls what it holds**: 0.7.15's first build found that when a piece it held fell due, the rollover sold the replacement to the bank, which funded it at the window and failed, so on Jerus's word, *"Build the rollover fix"*, it takes its maturing par again at issue as a non-competitive add-on at the issue's price, par for par, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's practice; past its dial it lets what it holds run off, as the Fed did under QT; and at 100% it takes the whole issue when the market's part is nothing (*"Yes, the backstop"*), which the Fed never does. And last year's surplus pays the market's part of what falls due first and then the central bank's par (*"Surplus pays everyone"*), so a city in surplus clears its paper whoever holds it; when a surplus pays only part of the par, the paper shrinks under the central bank and it ends that month over its dial, and the holdings step sells the excess to the bank — Jerus: *"Leave it (as built)"*.

The default city never owes paper at home, so the dial cannot be measured on it: its runs, and the autopilot's, are 0.7.14's to the byte. Where the dial bites, on eight seeds a setup: a Lean founding at 50% failed its bank 12 times and ended at 159,372 people on average, and at 100% 11 times and 156,877, paying all its paper off again between months 252 and 1,080 with the central bank rolling in only 10 months across the eight; held at 25%, where the spiral is, the city ended at 4,529 people with the dial at nothing, 5,626 at 50% and 1,047 at 100%, with 43, 105 and 61 failures. That first build's better 25% city at 100% — 9,476 people — was a loop: each rollover sold the bank about three times the maturing face for cash, and the central bank bought it back under face and remitted the gain. Par for par ended it. At 100% the central bank is the buyer when nobody else is; it does not limit what the city can sell. A 0.7.15 save with the dial past half, opened in 0.7.14, loads at half, and Jerus left it so. `CentralBankCheck`'s sections 17 to 20 assert the whole of the paper with the compression whole from half, the floor split by holder, the par taken again at issue, and the surplus paying the market's part first.

### The defence spends

Until 0.7.2 the vault damped a push on the currency and not a dollar left it: a capacity that cost nothing, which is why the default player never saw it work. Now the central bank **sells**. On a month the currency is pushed weaker and the city ran a deficit, it sells the vault's capacity times the month's own deficit — its current plus financial account when negative, in dollars at the month's rate, not the trailing window the push reads — and never more than the vault holds. What damps the push is the **realised** absorption, what was sold over what was wanted, so a full vault damps what its cover says, one running low damps less each month, and an empty one damps nothing. A push with no deficit that month sells and damps nothing; a rise is never met, because leaning against appreciation is buying dollars, which is a decision, not something a vault does by standing there.

```
push        = trade pressure + ratePressure        // ratePressure = −realRateDifferential × RATE_PULL, held within MAX_RATE_PRESSURE either way
absorption  = MAX_ABSORPTION × min(1, cover / COMFORTABLE_COVER)      // .85 at six months of imports
dollarsSold = min(absorption × deficitUsd, vault)          // only on a push to weaken, in a month that ran a deficit
realised    = dollarsSold / deficitUsd
rate        ×= 1 + push × (1 − realised) × openness × DRIFT_SPEED
rate        += (parity − rate) × REVERSION
```

**A capital transaction, not money destroyed.** The buyer is the world, and the local money it hands back is money the pools had already paid out for the imports: the deposit half of the textbook happened the day the goods were bought. So the vault falls by the dollars, the central bank's equity falls by their local price (`vaultSpent()`, a line under equity on the Money page, *spent defending the currency since founding*), M0 does not move, no pool moves and the audit declares nothing, and the month's profit and the remittance are untouched. It is booked at the reprice, after the audit, through `dollarsSold()`, with the month and the lifetime kept apart (`getDefendedThisMonth()`, `getDefendedLifetime()`). The first build retired the money instead and took seed 0's M0 to minus $255M, a bank that had destroyed more than it ever made. The Exchange page says what was sold this month and since founding, and the Trade tab's forces page shows the four terms that exist: trade, the real rate, the vault's defence and parity.

**What it did with the founders' billion**, when a city was founded on one (0.7.2), was spend it on structural deficits, not crises. On the eight seeds every one sold more than half of it and six all but 1%, over 22 to 225 sale months, half of it gone by month 628 to 3,747 — while the playtest's advisor buys it back with the treasury's cash, so that one seed sold US\$1.29B out of a US\$1B vault. `MAX_ABSORPTION` .85 at a `COMFORTABLE_COVER` of six months spends about 0.85 months of cover per deficit-sized month, so a vault at six months of cover meets the first deficit-sized month at full strength and damps less every month after, about half as hard five months in. On the default seed on 22 September the defence sold US\$1.06B in 174 months, the most US\$62.3M in month 725; half the founders' dollars were gone by month 726 and all but a hundredth by month 1,774, the vault ended at US\$134k, and \$531M of the central bank's equity went on it. Since 0.7.10 a city is founded on US\$25M, not a billion ([founding a city](#16-founding-a-city)), and the default playtest's vault was half gone by month 141 against 739 and empty by month 374 against 987, the defence spending US\$202M against US\$1,189M, while the worst currency month fell from 3.34 to 1.54 local to the dollar (0.7.10). On 28 September the defence sold US\$24.9M in 63 months, the most US\$3.7M in month 66; the vault was at its lowest, US\$973k, in month 973, half the founders' dollars were gone by month 753, \$17.3M of the central bank's equity went on it, and the advisor's purchases left US\$53.1M in the vault at the end. Whether the defence should answer only a crisis is Jerus's.

### The demand channel

For the rate to bite at home a household's saving has to answer the real return, and since 0.7.3 it does. What a household spends above a basket a head is scaled by one factor a month, struck on the **real deposit rate** — the bank's deposit rate less the year's inflation, `Game.realDepositRate()` — before the households plan. Deposits and not the curve, because the marginal saver's return is what the bank pays on every balance every month. Subsistence never moves; the propensity's share, the wealth term and the surplus the counter and the table spend out of all scale by it, so a hike does not hand what the grocer lost to the counter — scaling the want alone had pushed the surplus *up*, and a hike raised spending. At a factor of one every line is the old plan to the bit. Nothing is saved; the load path strikes it again. The monetary page says it in words: *"savers earn X% real, so households spend Y% of what they would at zero."*

```
spendFactor     = clamp(1 − SAVING_RESPONSE × realDepositRate, SPEND_FLOOR, SPEND_CEILING)
realDepositRate = the bank's deposit rate − the year's inflation
// SAVING_RESPONSE 1.0, provisional, Jerus's number · SPEND_FLOOR 0.5 · SPEND_CEILING 1.5
```

So the chain runs from the dial, to the deposit rate the bank chooses as a share of it (until 0.7.7, a share of what its book and its reserves earned), to the real deposit rate, to the factor, to the plan, to the shelf. `MonetaryCheck` section 6 — the assertion that had waited since the first batch — holds one founding at 3, 10, 20 and 40% from month 25 to 60 and asserts that **inflation falls with the rate**: each row no higher than the one before within `MEASUREMENT_NOISE`, and the 3% row at least `TRANSMISSION_FLOOR`, a point a year, above the 40% row. The noise was 0.05 points a year until 0.7.11, when a ten-year fixed mortgage that locks in the month it is written put the rows held a month late up to 0.053 apart, and on Jerus's word it is 0.10; on 28 September they differ by 0.000 to 0.035. It went green at 1.032 points on 0.7.3, where 0.7.2 read 0.996 and would have failed, read 1.428 on 0.7.7, and reads **1.304 points** on 28 September.

*MonetaryCheck section 6 on 28 September: one founding, the dial held from month 25 to 60*

| Dial | Inflation a year | Currency at month 60 | Deposit rate | Real deposit rate | Spend factor |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 3% | +0.04% | 0.9454 | 0.00% | −0.07% | 1.000 |
| 10% | −0.03% | 0.7409 | 3.49% | +3.17% | 0.968 |
| 20% | −0.55% | 0.5689 | 5.94% | +6.20% | 0.936 |
| 40% | −1.26% | 0.3516 | 13.21% | +14.16% | 0.858 |

> **The channel is in, and it moves very little**
>
> Most of that point is still the currency's: the rate moves inflation by making the currency dearer and imports cheaper, which it did before the channel existed. The channel fires every month and reaches almost nothing, for four reasons. **Weak pass-through.** Until 0.7.7 the bank paid savers `DEPOSIT_PASS_THROUGH`, 45%, of what it *earned*, not a rate, so the deposit rate carried about a quarter of the dial — 11% at a 40% dial — and the factor ran only from 0.99 to 0.88 across the whole range. Since 0.7.7 the bank passes on a share of the dial it chooses, and on 28 September the same founding's deposit rate ran from nothing at a 3% dial to 13.21% at 40%, and the factor from 1.000 to 0.858. **Nothing to act on in the index.** Food is four fifths of it, and the shelf does not answer money at the margin: at the founding it sits at its floor on every row, and in a grown city the want is thirty times what the shops can serve, so the scarcity mark-up reads the shops' coverage and a tenth less want moves no price. **The counter and the table are not in the index**, and that is where discretionary money goes. **Saved money compounds:** at a held high rate savings earn interest paid in new money, and the wealth term spends a fixed share of a stock growing faster than the factor cuts it. On 0.7.3's default eight the factor's median was 0.994; held at 10, 30 and 50% the six broke seeds swung 1.25×, 1.75× and 2.24× where they had swung 1.24×, 1.90× and 2.01×, and their index ended *higher* at 30 and 50%. A held high rate does not deflate through demand.
>
> *A demand channel needs a price that answers to demand.* The assertion is green on the transmission as a whole, not on this channel, and the next rate that bites will be a shelf priced by scarcity against money rather than coverage, or a deposit rate that passes more of the dial through.

### The dials

*Every number the money chapter turns on, with where it lives — the provisional ones are marked so in the source*

| Dial | Constant | Value | What it does |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| The policy rate | `DebtManager.MAX_POLICY_RATE` | 0–100% | the rate reserves earn; opens at the neutral 3%, chips 0 to 100 |
| The rule | `NEUTRAL_RATE` · `inflationTarget` · `TAYLOR_WEIGHT` | 3% · 2% · 1.5 | what the autopilot sets, at the default target: 7.5% at 5% inflation, 67.5% at 45% |
| The target | `DebtManager.DEFAULT_INFLATION_TARGET` · `MAX_INFLATION_TARGET` | 2% · 20% | the player's since 0.7.4, in half points from nothing; 10% at most until 0.7.15; the strip's colours read from it |
| The window | `CentralBank.WINDOW_PENALTY` | ¼ point | over the dial, on what the bank borrows past its deposits; a point until 0.7.7 |
| What savers get | `Bank.DEPOSIT_SHARE_FLUSH` · `DEPOSIT_SHARE_AT_WINDOW` · `DEPOSIT_RATE_SPEED` | .35 · .90 · ⅙ | the share of the dial the bank passes on when flush and when at the window, and how far it moves a month; 45% of its interest income until 0.7.7 |
| The advances ceiling | `advancesCeilingMonths` | 6 mo | 0 to `MAX_ADVANCES_CEILING` 36 months of the treasury's revenue, averaged over `REVENUE_MONTHS` 12 |
| The holdings dial | `CentralBank.targetShare` | 0–100% | of the term paper; `MAX_QE_SHARE` 1.0 since 0.7.15, .5 before |
| Its pace | `QE_SPEED` | .25 | of the largest of the dial, the setting before it and the share held, a month |
| What holding buys | `QE_COMPRESSION` · `FULL_COMPRESSION_SHARE` | 1.0 · .5 | the whole term premium once half the term paper is held, and nothing more past it |
| The term premium | `TERM_PREMIUM_10Y` … `50Y` | .50–1.50 pt | provisional; see [debt](#12-the-citys-borrowing) |
| The saving response | `HouseholdBalance.SAVING_RESPONSE` | 1.0 | provisional; the factor held between `SPEND_FLOOR` .5 and `SPEND_CEILING` 1.5 |
| The real rate's pull | `ForeignAccounts.RATE_PULL` | 4 | provisional; six until 0.7.2; `MAX_RATE_PRESSURE` 4.0 is a guard at a hundred points |
| The hot money's appetite | `CapitalFlows.MAX_SPREAD` | .25 | provisional; .06 until 0.7.2 |
| The defence | `MAX_ABSORPTION` · `COMFORTABLE_COVER` | .85 · 6 mo | the share of a deficit a full vault meets, and the cover that counts as full |
| The currency's guards | `ForeignAccounts.MIN_RATE` · `MAX_RATE` | 1e-9 · 1e9 | numerical guards, scaled by a reform; .01 and 100 until 0.7.3 |

The chapter's harnesses are `CentralBankCheck` (twenty sections: the identity, the floor, the window, the note's price, advances and the ceiling, the arrears rule, the autopilot, the save and a reform, the holdings dial and the ceiling dial, and since 0.7.15 the whole of the paper, the floor split by holder, the par taken again at issue and the surplus paying everyone), `HoldersCheck`, `CurrencyCheck`, `MonetaryCheck` section 6, `CreditCheck` section 11 and `TreasuryCheck`, and they are listed in [how it's checked](#22-how-its-checked). The central bank's month is not saved, so after a reload the Money page's *this month* lines read nothing until the month turns; that is on the list too.

## 15. Prices, the currency & the world

*The city has a price level, a currency with a name, a vault of dollars, a balance of payments, hot money that comes for the spread, a rent market that no longer follows wages, and — since the surplus had nowhere to go — somewhere for its savings to sit.*

### A price index, and prices that ration

A fixed basket — the shelf price and rent, weighted by what households actually spent in a base month two years after the city started shopping — is the city's price level. The basket does not re-weight to hide inflation. The shelf price is cost-plus and rises to 1.6× at total shortage, so a congested city spends more at the shops for fewer goods, and the household screen says who went short.

**The index remembers its own high and low water-marks**, and the month each was set. An end-of-run figure says where a city finished, not what it lived through: a run that ends at 0.98 having been at 1.31 and 0.62 is not the same city as one that never moved, and until the marks were kept there was no way to tell them apart from the outside. The pair and the swing between them are carried in the save; a city saved before the marks existed opens with both sitting on today's level, which is the only honest thing to say about a past nobody recorded.

**Rent is two markets**: family homes and studios, each with a cost floor from the cheapest template *that serves that segment*, at today's cash and materials prices spread over a landlord's yield of 5.8%, times that segment's households per front door, unbounded both ways, closing a twelfth of the gap a month because a lease is twelve months. Taking one floor across the whole portfolio and applying it to both legs was what turned rent into a constant — every building earning the same $445 a head whatever it cost, and a city that built 138 low-rise blocks and no studios with 1,847 households wanting one. Struck per segment, studio rent went $445 to $706 and studio doors over 4,000 months went from zero to 19,920. Land is deliberately *not* in the floor: land price is a capitalised rent, an output of this market, and feeding it back in grew a number because it grew. Overbuild and rent falls below cost and the landlords eat it.

### The city's dollar, and what moves it

The local currency was the **Danzik dollar, D\$**, until 0.7.10, and since then it is the city's own: named after the city by default — a city founded as Arden pays in the Arden dollar, A\$, ARD — or by hand, with a three-letter code that is never USD, and a save from before loads as Danzik, in the Danzik dollar, D\$, DZD. This page writes D\$ for it, against the US dollar. Since 0.7.2 its rate moves on three things: pressure from the balance of payments; the **real** rate differential, `Game.realRateDifferential()` — the policy rate less the city's inflation, against the world's base rate less the world's realised inflation — at `RATE_PULL` 4 a point, so money moves toward the higher real return; and a pull toward relative parity (`REVERSION`, a fifteen-year half-life) that says where the rate should end up. The drift that moved it every month by the whole of the inflation differential, `rate *= 1 + (local − world) / 12`, is **deleted**. With imports repricing through the rate, wages chasing the whole index and the shelf cost-plus, a gain of one on that link meant a city whose prices rose 40% a year saw its currency fall 40% a year by rule, whatever its central bank did; Jerus's 0.6.9 city, 399× its founding prices in twenty-five years, was that loop run for 306 months. The inflation differential still reaches the currency, through parity, which rises with local prices, and through the trade balance a cheap or dear currency earns — but not month by month, by rule. **A spiral needs an actual outflow to continue, and a credible real rate stops it:** in `CurrencyCheck`, ten months of 40% inflation with the real gap at nothing move the rate to 1.0067, the parity pull alone, where the drift would have taken it to 1.3649. The world has its own inflation, a persistent moving average drawn low in 1–8%, deterministic, with its level pulled back to trend so that 333-year runs stay usable.

```
current account   exports − imports − interest paid abroad − foreign savers' interest
financial account what the city's owners send abroad, less what comes home
position          reserves − foreign debt   // revaluation lives here, not on any statement
real rate gap     (policy − inflation) − (world base − world inflation)   // RATE_PULL 4 a point
hot money         spread = max(depositRate, cityRate) − worldRate − countryPremium   // at most MAX_SPREAD
```

The caps on the channel are numerical guards now: `MAX_RATE_PRESSURE` went from .8 to 4.0 and binds only at a hundred-point real gap, and the hot money's appetite, `CapitalFlows.MAX_SPREAD`, from .06 to .25, measured, until 0.7.7 took the strain premium out of every rate, against the city's rate net of it (`getRateBeforeStrain()`, gone with it), because what a strained bank charges is not a return. `RATE_PULL` went from 6 to 4, the one retune the batch allowed itself: at six the loop's gain was 1.44 against the deleted drift's 1.0, and one seed whose dial sat at 0.08% went to the guard with its prices at 115× founding; at four the gain is 0.96, and no default seed goes near a guard. The cost is that a credible real rate buys two thirds of the support it did. *The channel is only as good as the hand on the dial.* The Trade tab's forces page shows the four terms that exist — trade, the real rate, the vault's defence and parity — and what the reprice was handed rides the foreign accounts' saved array, the defence at slots 25–27 and the real differential with its two inflations at 28–30, so the page survives a reload.

**And since 0.7.3 there is no guard a player will meet.** `ForeignAccounts.MAX_RATE` and `MIN_RATE` were 100 and .01 and pinned the currency — the last acts of Jerus's year book were a currency at its guard with imports no longer rising — and they are 1e9 and 1e-9 now, scaled by a reform: a guard against a rate run to nothing or to infinity, never a price the game expects to see. Past a hundredth of a cent the strip's second line turns round and says what a US cent costs, *US¢1 = D$1,000* at a rate of 100,000, instead of printing 0.00¢, and every page prints a rate through one formatter (`Money.fxRate()`). On the default seed on 22 September its dearest dollar was 1.000 local, in month 2; it spent no month weaker than twice parity and none at a guard, prices averaged +0.05% a year, and the run ended with the rate at 0.482 local to the dollar, 53% under a parity of 1.016. On 28 September its dearest dollar was again 1.000 local in month 2, with no month weaker than twice parity and none at a guard; prices averaged +0.04% a year, and the rate ended at 0.632, 37% under a parity of 1.006.

### The vault

**The founders leave one.** Jerus: *"of the 3.5B you start with, 1B is in usd in the reserve, so you only see 2.5B start with"* — because 99% of players would never buy reserves. From 0.6.10 to 0.7.9 a new city opened with D\$2.5B in the treasury and US\$1B in the vault, and since 0.7.10 it opens with D\$100M and US\$25M, the IMF's old three months of imports for a town of eight to ten thousand ([founding a city](#16-founding-a-city)); the dollars are bought on day one at the opening rate and booked as the purchase they are (`Game.FOUNDING_CASH`, `FOUNDING_RESERVE_USD`), and for the city's first ten years the Exchange page says where they came from. **It is kept in dollars.** Checking the founding reserve found it in the wrong currency: it was a local figure at the price paid, so a hundredfold fall turned a US\$1B vault into US\$10M and its import cover fell with it, while the dollar debt beside it was revalued every month. The stock is dollars now, its local value the dollars times the rate, cover no longer moves with the currency, and the month's move is a revaluation line, not cash and not an audit flow. The treasury still buys and sells reserves, and since 0.7.6 the land office can be paid straight out of the vault ([land](#17-land)); the central bank reads the vault as its asset and, since 0.7.2, spends it defending the currency ([the central bank](#14-the-central-bank)).

**A reserve defends a currency; it does not hold one down.** Jerus's rule, chosen from three after the founding reserve caused the very year book it was meant to prevent. The vault used to damp the pressure on the rate both ways, so a deep one muted the surplus a weak currency earns and the support of the policy rate — the two forces that pull a currency out of a spiral — and with the founders' dollars in it three of eight seeds reproduced Jerus's city, two of them past 140× their founding prices with the currency at its guard. It damps only a push weaker now, and the eight went to a median price swing of 1.60×, none past 2.81×, with sudden stops 8 to 0.

**And the strip carries them.** Between the population and the cash sit three panels. Prices against founding, over inflation year on year. The rate both ways in the currency's own names, *US\$1 = D\$x* over *D\$1 = US¢y*, grey at or above parity and down to 5% under it, amber more than 5% below it and red past 25%. And since 0.7.4 *the price of money*, Jerus: *"on the top of the UI the bank rate, the central bank rate, both should be shown, as well as the rate you borrow in"* — three lines at the caption's weight, *central* the dial, *bank* the bank's lending rate on it, reading *no bank* or *failed* in red when the bank lends nothing, and *city* what the treasury borrows at; lines and not three figures, because three figures at the population's weight would be the loudest panel on the strip, and the date and the money stay the loudest things. The inflation readout was grey within three points of the 2% target, amber outside it and red past 10% either way. Since 0.7.15 it reads from the player's target: grey within three points either side of it, amber three to five points over it or more than three under, and red more than five over (`STRIP_INFLATION_OVER_TARGET`, Jerus: *"Red at target + 5 points"*) or with prices falling faster than 10% a year, whatever the target; at the default target, inflation of 7 to 10% read amber and reads red now. Every figure comes through a getter, and the strip recomputes nothing.

### The surplus, and where it goes

A city that exports steel used to run a surplus of 30–50% of GDP with nowhere for it to go: no household bought anything abroad, nobody was paid a dividend, and no saver could own a foreign asset. The currency simply appreciated — about 10% a year, 1.20 down to 0.44 over 250 months — until every exporter in the city was dead, twenty times a run.

**Outward investment** is the door. A sector with an idle till buys the world's paper when the world pays more than the bank — forty times the spread, up to nine tenths of its wealth, moving 4% of the gap a month out and 10% home — and brings it home to fund a plan, pay a dividend or clear an overdraft. Households run the identical rule on their own savings. The coupon is *rolled where it is earned*, an income credit matched by a financial debit, so a rentier's surplus does not appreciate the currency, and the currency is priced on the whole balance rather than the trade half. The median run went from 33% below parity to 3.5%; exports went $33M to $124M a month. Since 0.7.12 a sector that owes nothing also puts a share of its wealth into the other sectors' bonds by the same rule, never its own, and still most of it goes abroad: after 0.7.12's eight default runs the companies held $6.7T abroad against $1.7T in their tills.

**And since 17 September the households spend abroad too**, through three doors the surplus did not have. A car the city did not make is an import at the ceiling; a watch always is, deliberately, so that wanting luxuries is money that leaves rather than going round again, and import substitution, if it ever comes, is something a player achieves; and every tonne the railway hauls burns fuel priced in the world's money, charged as a real import before there is any oil good, so that a reform cannot forget it. A meal is the exception — the food in it was already counted when it crossed the border, and the margin is wages and rent here.

**Hot money** comes for the spread net of the risk, at 8% of the gap a month, and leaves at 20%, straight into and out of the bank's deposits — which are its lending capacity, so the boom and the sudden stop are procyclical by construction. A run needs a *fragile* position (a material stock of it with under 25% backed by reserves) *and* a shock: the currency down 12% in a year, the bank insolvent, or a recent default. Always painful, never fatal.

Who owns the bank is a curve of financial deepening: a city with no savings has no domestic investors, a city with $124B on deposit owns its own banks. The bank's capital follows that curve. Its wholesale funding followed it too, which is what stopped a $156B book declaring its entire funding cost as interest paid abroad, until 0.7.0 moved the funding to the central bank's window, where the interest is paid at home and declared as money destroyed.

### The policy rate, and dropping zeros

The policy rate is the player's dial, with an advisory Taylor rule beside it saying what it would do and why, obeying the Taylor principle — and since 0.7.0 an autopilot that hands the rule the dial; the dial itself, and everything it now moves, is [the central bank](#14-the-central-bank). The playtest works the dial a quarter of the way toward the advice each time, because a rate that sat at 3% for three centuries would leave the whole monetary half untested. And once the city's own price index passes ten times founding, a **currency reform** unlocks: divide everything by 10, 100 or 1,000, the player's choice, never automatic. Every money constant in the game is an instance field seeded from its constant and redenominated with everything else; foreign prices are the exception, quoted in someone else's money and reached through the rate. The reform instant is bit-exact and conserves money; the following month is a few percent adrift in the discrete decisions, which is filed and has a plan.

## 16. Founding a city

*Until 0.7.10 every city was the same city at month zero: Danzik, founded on D\$2.5B and US\$1B, with no reason ever to borrow. A player founds a city now — its name, its money, what it starts with and the world's inflation — and the default start is small enough that the city borrows for what it builds.*

Jerus: *"lets reduce the cash the city starts with, both the foreign usd and the starting cash, what do you think makes sense? cause the city should borrow right"*. A trace of 0.7.9 found the treasury never going below D\$2.467B in thirty years: the young city spent \$0.1–2M a month and took in \$0.4–5M, owed nothing for about ninety years, and held a vault of 270 or more months of its imports. The endowment had been sized on 9 September to buy the opening, a coal power plant, and nothing since had asked it to do less. **Since 0.7.10 a city is founded on D\$100M and US\$25M**, Jerus's choice from the options put to him (`Game.FOUNDING_CASH`, `FOUNDING_RESERVE_USD`): the treasury founds the village and one of the first big works, and the city borrows for the rest, the way towns pay for long-lived works, on bonds repaid over the asset's life — Britain's New Towns were built on sixty-year loans from the Exchequer, not on endowments. The vault follows the IMF's old rule of three months of imports. The endowment is still a game number, and the code says so.

**The sticker is not the invoice.** What a new city pays for a building is the building and the material beyond its yard at the world's price: the water plant's D\$65.8M is invoiced D\$109.6M. So D\$100M buys the founding village, D\$32.9M, and one of the wind farm, the school or the police station; the option Jerus picked had been described on stickers, and he kept D\$100M once it was described on invoices, so the water plant is a bond from day one. That is why the build screen offers a twenty-year bond sized to the gap ([the city's borrowing](#12-the-citys-borrowing)): a Standard city a year on is D\$26.1M short of the water plant, issues D\$40.3M of face at 4.22%, raises D\$26.13M, pays about D\$56k a month, and has the plant in 57 months with the audit closing every month (`NewGameCheck`, section 11).

### Found a city

Jerus, the same afternoon: *"a small thing at the start of the game where you choose the name of the city and the currency … and perhaps the settings to choose the starting cash and usd cash and offworld inflation rate … (with option to just start at default)"*. *Start New Game* opens **Found a city** (`ui/FoundingScreen`): the city's name; its money, named after the city or, with a tick, by hand, a name and three letters that are never USD; the money it is founded with; the world's inflation, moved there from Settings because it acts only at founding; and *Found with defaults*, which founds straight away. Each start shows what it buys, at the invoices a new city will actually pay.

*The starts, in the order the page lists them (`Founding`)*

| Start | Treasury | Vault | What it is |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Insane | D$0 | US$0 | since 0.7.14: the ground it stands on owed abroad, a twenty-year dollar bond at 3% for US$2,100k |
| Lean | D$25M | US$10M | three quarters of the founding village; the city borrows from its first months |
| Standard | D$100M | US$25M | the default: the village and one of the first big works |
| Wealthy | D$2.5B | US$1B | the start every city had from 0.6.10 to 0.7.9 |
| Custom | D\$5M–D\$10B | US\$0–US\$4B | for testing, not balanced for play |

The choice is a record on the city (`Founding`), set once, saved under eight keys and never changed; the currency is a value per city, read through `game.getCurrency()`, because one process holds several cities — the harnesses', and the playtest's reloaded twin. The window's title and the save lists name the city, and every screen that prints its money names it. A save from before 0.7.10 loads as Danzik, in the Danzik dollar, founded on D\$2.5B and US\$1B, which is what it was. A new game also founds on the autopilot and with the rollover on *same structure* since 0.7.13, and with the bank's resolution automatic since 0.7.14; an older save keeps what it was played with. Building the screen found two bugs on the founding path: a new game after a load kept the loaded world's inflation, and a new city's first year was back-cast at the previous city's rate.

### Insane

Jerus: *"on game start, add a new difficulty called Insane, which is just you start with 0 cash, 0 vault, and a 20y bond 3% for the initial land cost … if easier the starting debt is abroad in usd"*. Since 0.7.14 it is the first start on the page: D\$0, US\$0, and a twenty-year dollar bond at 3% owed abroad for the starting land — 3,000,000 square feet at the land market's opening price of US\$0.70 a square foot, US\$2,100k. No cash moves, because the founders' land was bought on it, and on the world's curve it is worth US\$375k on day 0. The founding card quotes day 0 for the village, a city with no revenue and no output paying the full spread: the twenty-year bond at 13.90%, \$85,500k of face to raise \$32,978k, the six-month note at 13.00%, and the window abroad shut. 0.7.14 made the clock refuse to run until such a city had borrowed (Jerus: *"Borrow first"*); since 0.7.15 it runs on the central bank's advances from its first month instead ([the central bank](#14-the-central-bank)).

Of 0.7.14's eight Insane seeds, three became cities of 148,000, 206,000 and 148,000 people, and five spiralled on the city's own paper, ending with 3,686 to 10,118 people and \$420T to \$6,416T of it; the playtest's player borrows exactly the village's invoice, so every seed ran on the advances from month 3. Lean is hard too: D\$25M covers three quarters of the village, every seed borrows by month 4 to 14, and on 0.7.10 half of them ran out of cash around month 140 and lived on the advances for 450 to 500 months.

### What the smaller start did

As 0.7.10 measured it, making the founding a choice changed nothing else: founded Wealthy, the city reproduced three old ensembles byte for byte, all 24 seed-runs. The default playtest never borrows on D\$100M; its treasury bottoms out at D\$61–67M in its first two years and then grows. What the default run does show is the vault, half gone by month 141 against 739 and empty by month 374 against 987. Under the autopilot the bank failed 76 times against 49, and all of the rise was the vault's: D\$100M with the old US\$1B vault gave the old counts, and D\$2.5B with US\$25M the new ones, because without dollars to steady the currency a rule-held rate sees more imported inflation in the city's middle years. Held at 10%, every seed now runs dry in years 185 to 253, where three of eight did before: a city held at that rate loses money for centuries, and the D\$2.4B had been paying for it. And 42 fixtures in 25 harnesses had been living on the old treasury without saying so — ten went red and three were green only because they ran on a short calendar — and each funds itself explicitly now, with no premise and no tolerance moved.

## 17. Land

*The city starts with thirty blocks, allocated so that a power station and a water plant leave two spare — land is taught on turn one.*

Nine plots are on offer at any time (`LandMarket.LISTING_SIZE`; earlier editions said ten), generated deterministically from the plot's own id, so parcel 47 is the same plot in every session and in every reload. Sizes are multiples of a floor that rises with how much the city already owns; 15% of plots are enormous tracts, and the tract is what makes the listing worth reading.

### Two prices, moved by different things

```
what the city pays     a base per sq ft in US dollars, raised by blocks already owned and by population — the two premiums no longer multiply — at the day's rate
what businesses pay   the same base and premiums in the city's own money, × a scarcity multiplier from 0.65 to 1.90 on allocated/available
```

The multiplier passes 1.0 at about 61% built — below that the city sells land at a loss, which is the intended cost of over-annexing. The earlier version multiplied by utilisation, which sat between 86% and 100% for 2,400 straight months, so "scarcity" was decoration. From 9 September the city was founded with a **\$3.5B endowment** — D\$2.5B in the treasury and US\$1B in the vault from 0.6.10 — enough for a coal plant at 41% of it, a works department at 400 points a month, a shed of material, and a bank standing on day one. Since 0.7.10 it is D\$100M and US\$25M, and the big works are borrowed for ([founding a city](#16-founding-a-city)).

### Land is bought in dollars

Jerus: *"when you buy land, make it so that it costs USD not domestic currency, and basically how it would work is a little toggle at the top to choose, when you buy land, to use up your USD reserves or to convert cash into usd exactly to buy the land, and the default is that you convert."* Since 0.7.6 the land office prices every parcel in US dollars — the same base and premiums, so at the founding rate of 1.00 every number is what it was — fixed when it is listed, and the treasury pays usd × rate on the day it buys: a weak currency makes land dear and a strong one cheap. What businesses pay the city stays local money, struck exactly as before, so the city's margin on land carries the currency, and a currency reform no longer clears the office's board. There are two ways to pay, a chip pair at the top of the office. **Converting**, the default: the treasury buys exactly the dollars and hands them over in one movement, and the vault ends where it began. **From the vault**: the dollars leave it and no local money moves, a capital transaction like the defence's, and the treasury's journal carries the land back against the budget's land line. A vault too short for the plot spends what it holds and converts the rest, and the receipt says so. On the default seed on 28 September the advisor paid US\$10.2B abroad for land over 151 months, none of it out of the vault, and it cost D\$6.15B at the day's rates, 39.6% less than it would have at the founding rate.

Since 0.7.13 the office speaks the paying currency and square kilometres — Jerus: *"for the land … instead of blocks, say km^2, and add a button to buy multiple"*. A plot's large price is in local money when converting and in US dollars from the vault, with the other as a caption beside it; areas read in km² on the exact international foot, to three figures, so a block is 0.00929 km², and so do the Summary's land panel, the build screen's *Not enough land* page and the time-skip report. A plot the city cannot afford no longer refuses: its button opens a funding page built from the build screen's own pieces — converting, the twenty-year bond sized to the gap and the six-month note; from the vault, a twenty-year dollar bond or a six-month dollar note sized to the dollar gap, whose dollars are held in the vault, or the old top-up from cash; with the window abroad shut, the reason and only what remains. And *Buy the next N plots*, five by default, buys the office's first N, cheapest ground a square foot first; because a listed plot's price is frozen, buying them at once costs exactly what buying them one by one does. Converting for land has never pushed the currency, which is on the list.

**Ground is what a mature city runs out of** — land sits at 88–90% for the last decade of most long runs — and the newest sectors are the hungriest for it. A Rail Terminal is 5,500,000 square feet, nearly three times a Coal Power Plant and the largest footprint in the catalogue; a Livestock Farm is 120 acres, the dearest ground of any farm at $108k an acre; a Metro Line is 30,000 square feet for thirty thousand journeys a month, five hundred times a gravel road's capacity per acre. That ladder is the whole reason the modes exist — see [transport](#20-transport--vehicles). Every sector's planner assumes the ground is free and none of them can see they are bidding for the same land; that is on the list.

**Iron is a pooled resource.** A parcel carries a deposit *count* and a tonnage; deposits cap how many mines can stand, and every mine draws from one reserve. Roughly 28% of ore parcels carry more than one site. Ore in the ground is worth a fraction of what it fetches once it is out — the value is in getting it out — and a deposit that is worked out closes its mine inside a year, which is what makes the bust when a mining city runs dry a real event rather than a slow leak.

## 18. The catalogue

*Seventy-three buildings in `buildings.json`, hot-editable next to the game, every one on a sourced real capital cost at the size the game actually builds it. Edit a number, restart, look — no rebuild. Ids are permanent, because saves are keyed by them; the next is 73, and eighteen were added in the three days to 18 September.*

| Category | Templates | What it does |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Residential | 3 | House (six), Studio Apartments (two), Low-Rise (four) — a home has a size and a household has to fit it |
| Commercial | 3 | Convenience Store, Small Grocery — coverage is how many people can shop — and the Commercial Bank |
| Industrial | 5 | Industrial Bakery and Bakery, which buy crops and bake bread and bakery goods out of them (until September 2026 they were a Textile Mill and a Food Processing Plant making a good called Food out of nothing); and the eleventh sector's Meat Works, Snack & Oils Plant and Bottling Plant — five, six and four posts, among the smallest investor-built job steps in the catalogue |
| Heavy industry | 5 | Steel Foundry and Steel Mini-Mill, plus manufacturing's Fabrication Shop, Fabrication Works and Machine Works — the first domestic customer steel ever had |
| Business services | 3 | Contact Centre, Shared Services Centre, Engineering Services Office — seats sold abroad; the last needs licensed engineers before it will open |
| Agriculture | 4 | Mixed Farm, Grain Farm, Greenhouse Complex and, since 16 September, the Livestock Farm — 13.8, 55, 3.4 and 120 acres; the glass is the one that survives expensive ground, and the herd is the dearest of the farms per acre — $108k against the Grain Farm's $22k — and sells 6.5% of its build cost a month against the Grain Farm's 18% |
| Mining | 1 | Iron Mine — sixty jobs, a quarry lifting 30,000 t/yr |
| Construction | 2 | Construction Depot, and the Construction Materials Plant — the seventh sector's only building |
| Electricity | 2 | Coal Power Plant — 280 MW at $1.43B, far more than a city of 74,000 needs — and a Wind Farm, the first small plant beside it |
| Water | 1 | Water Treatment Plant |
| Infrastructure | 6 | Gravel Road, Paved Road, Elevated Highway — each the cheapest per trip across a band of land prices — and since 16 September the Bus Network, Light Rail Line and Metro Line, the same ladder two rungs on: 2,500, 8,000 and 30,000 journeys a month, and the first things in this category that ever had a payroll |
| Rail | 3 | Rail Spur, Freight Line, Rail Terminal — 50,000, 200,000 and 500,000 tonnes a month across the city boundary at $140M, $520M and $1.24B, owned by the twelfth sector and financed like a steel mill; a terminal is 1,482 jobs on 5,500,000 square feet, the largest hiring commitment and the largest footprint in the game |
| Automotive | 4 | Vehicle Works and Assembly Plant (120 and 500 cars a month), Commercial Vehicle Plant (150 vans), Locomotive Works (four wagon sets) — all fed on fabricated steel and machinery, and anchored on heavy manufacturing's revenue per head rather than the food plants', because the first draft never cleared the interest test |
| Luxury | 2 | Boutique and Department Store — 320 and 4,200 pieces a month over a counter, importing every one of them |
| Hospitality | 2 | Diner and Restaurant — 13,500 and 40,500 meals a month, each buying the Convenience Store's basket scaled to the person-months its meals come to, to the kilogram |
| Healthcare | 14 | childcare, general, senior and death care, grouped by function in the menu |
| Education | 9 | three basic stages, college, university, and four professional schools that each license one job |
| Safety | 4 | two police buildings and two prisons — the city pays for all four |

Every building declares a cash cost, construction points, materials, maintenance, capacity, lot footprint in square feet, electricity and water draw, road load, its job mix across eleven types, and — since the template — **which sector owns it and what it makes and uses**. A healthcare building also declares what it treats, a school what it teaches, a safety building whether it is a station or a cell block, a transit line the journeys it can carry and a rail building the tonnes. The road load is one number and it is read as three: fitted to the catalogue itself, 0.726 × jobs + 0.878 × homes + 0.0386 × tonnes a month, so a mine keeps its 420 and learns that 68% of it is ore, a university is all commuters, and a shop's freight is a van at a back door. Money throughout is in thousands: a cash cost of 30 is $30,000. Every row of the build menu prices itself — sticker and all-in, from the same method that charges — and opens a card that explains the building from its own numbers.

> **Both halves of a price are sourced now**
>
> A unit of construction material was \$2,000 and is **\$18,000**, defined by the House: ten units against a real house's \$180,000 of structure. Every template's split was re-derived at a real material share — 40% for a building, 25% for a plant, 60% for a road — with every total held to the dollar. It also found that the builders' material import bill had never been paid: \$2.75bn crossed the border over 4,000 months and the expense struck at zero, so Construction ended every run holding the money and the balance of payments never saw a unit move. Range runs from a Home Daycare with two staff to a Rail Terminal with 1,482 jobs, the Regional Medical Centre's 996 the largest the city pays for, and the terminal's 5,500,000 square feet the largest footprint in the game, ahead of the Livestock Farm and a Municipal Cemetery's 2,000,000.

## 19. Utilities & roads

### Power and water

The grid starts with 10,000 W free and the reservoir with 8,000 units. Both are gated by the same utility workforce. Power is $0.01 a watt, water $0.05 a unit — about $5 per thousand gallons.

**Only businesses are invoiced.** Houses, depots, roads, the water plant's own 900 watts and the city's own buildings all draw power nobody pays for. Booking revenue on the whole city's draw was money from nowhere scaling with the housing stock — 73% of it, measured. The utility books exactly what its customers' statements charged them, not a recomputation at the end-of-month ratio.

### Roads

The city starts with 400 units of capacity — the streets that already exist. Traffic flows freely to 90% of capacity and degrades after that, floored at 35%. Three roads, and the land ladder was in the catalogue before anybody pointed at it: a gravel road is 500 square feet per unit of capacity, a paved road 208, an elevated highway 42 — twelve times the capacity per acre for two and a half times the money. Since 16 September the load is three streams and the network can be relieved by a highway, a tram or a train, but never deleted; that is [transport](#20-transport--vehicles), and this is the baseline it is measured against.

```
throughput = 1                      if load ≤ 0.9 × cap
           = max(0.35, 0.9/util)   otherwise
```

Congestion slowing the sites is the pointed part: a jammed city builds the roads that would unjam it more slowly, and the floor is what keeps that from being a trap.

### Construction output

```
round(capacity × construction fill rate × road ratio × health work ratio)
```

One definition, used by the screen, by the sites, and by what the sector is paid for. The three had to be the same number: a copy that drifts books revenue for work nobody did, and very nearly did when roads arrived. What reaches the *sites* is what is left once the standing stock has had its repairs — about 40% of the total, permanently.

## 20. Transport & vehicles

*Until 16 September the entire transport model was one scalar: a road network with a capacity and a load, one throughput ratio between 0.35 and 1, and three road types that were the same road at three prices. Jerus:* "decomposing the existing import/export bands into world price + transportation cost… then later, transportation efficiency can make that freight component smaller or larger." *Nine batches followed in three days under the same version number, each one there to make the next possible: the band decomposes, the load splits, the modes and the fare, the railway, the vehicles, and the screen that finally shows a player any of it.*

### The band was a freight bill

Every traded good carried two constants and the gap between them was the whole local market — and nothing in the game said why the gap was the width it was. Each good carries a third number now, the cost of moving one unit, and the two ends split into four:

```
worldImportPrice = worldBuyPrice  + baseFreight     // the world's own ask, plus getting it here
worldExportPrice = worldSellPrice − baseFreight     // the world's own bid, less getting it there
```

Three quarters of the wedge is freight and one quarter the world's margin, and the split is a game decision rather than a measurement: it sets how much of the band good logistics can ever win back. At three quarters a 23% band bottoms out near 6%. **The price table was already a freight model and nobody designed it that way**: freight as a share of the world price sits at 21–25% for fifteen of the seventeen goods that had both ends, and the two outside that band are iron at 49% and materials at 43% — the two lowest-value-density things in the game, where real freight genuinely is half the delivered cost. The delivered prices are the stored literals and the world band is derived, which is the opposite of how it reads and the only way round that is exact: storing the world band and adding the freight back gives 0.8470000000000002 for steel and 0.27999999999999997 for crops, and an ulp in this codebase is never nothing. Not one price moved on the day it shipped, and eight seeds over 333 years came back byte-identical; `TradeCostCheck` asserts every delivered price against a table of what it was that morning, because a test that reads its own subject proves nothing.

### One road load is three

`Traffic { COMMUTERS, GOODS, BULK }`, and which mode can carry what falls out of the classes rather than needing a table of exceptions: commuters can ride a tram and nothing else can; goods — a shop's bread and milk — are a van at a back door however many rails a city lays, and take the train only across the boundary; bulk — ore, steel, crops, grain, aggregate, beams, machines, a locomotive on a low-loader — is what a railway is for. The shares were fitted rather than guessed, by least squares against the catalogue itself:

```
roadLoad = 0.726 × jobs + 0.878 × homes + 0.0386 × tonnes a month        // R² = 0.74 over the 56 templates that loaded a road when the fit was struck; seventy do today
```

The implied rate is one worker per nineteen tonnes a month — a truckload — and nobody set out to encode that. The residuals are all explainable and all one way: an Iron Mine 280 over the fit (heavy vehicles), a Penitentiary 288 under and a Long-Term Care Complex 136 under (their occupants do not commute), a University 258 over (students travel and the fit counts only wages). None of it matters, because the fit supplies the *share* and the stored road load supplies the *magnitude*: a mine keeps its 420 and learns that 68% of it is ore.

*Commuters / goods / bulk, as the fit reads the catalogue*

| Building | Road load | Split |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Steel Mini-Mill | 500 | 17% / 0% / 83% |
| Grain Farm | 18 | 14% / 0% / 86% |
| Iron Mine | 420 | 32% / 0% / 68% |
| Bakery | 40 | 53% / 16% / 31% |
| Small Grocery | 55 | 87% / 12% / 1% |
| University | 520 | 100% / 0% / 0% |
| A played city | — | 86% / 3% / 11% |

A real city is 86% people, which is what urban traffic actually is. And the ensemble found a defect whose fix is the better design: the first version summed the three streams to get the network's total, and eight seeds came back subtly different from the build before them — a thousand dollars in three trillion, one person in forty-eight thousand — because every building's three loads add to its own road load to the bit, and what does not survive is adding them up in a different *order*. So the total keeps the exact sweep it always had and the breakdown is read alongside it. The demand did not change; only the ability to see what it is made of.

### The modes, and a fare that is a price

*The land ladder, per unit of capacity — a journey a month for the transit lines*

| Mode | Capacity | Land | Sq ft a unit | Cash a unit |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Gravel Road | 900 | 450,000 | 500 | $2,584 |
| Paved Road | 1,200 | 250,000 | 208 | $4,500 |
| Elevated Highway | 1,500 | 63,000 | 42 | $6,400 |
| Bus Network | 2,500 | 20,000 | 8 | $4,800 |
| Light Rail Line | 8,000 | 45,000 | 6 | $8,000 |
| Metro Line | 30,000 | 30,000 | 1 | $10,667 |

A metro is five hundred times a gravel road's capacity per acre for four times the price a journey. A city that has run out of ground and not out of money builds one; a city with ground to spare never should — which is the first real answer this game has had to its own late-game wall. **Every mode is a relief on an unchanged baseline**, and that is the design rather than an implementation detail: a city with no highway and no transit computes exactly the load it computed yesterday and degrades on exactly the curve it degraded on. A highway relieves freight, not by carrying more but because a tonne of ore on a grade-separated road does not share a junction with a school run — bulk by 40%, goods by 15%, commuters not at all. Transit takes people off the road entirely, and three things stop it being the answer to everything: at most 65% of commuters ever ride, whatever is built; what transit can carry is capped at twice the road capacity under it, because buses are road vehicles and a metro station needs a street outside it — *a city that builds a metro and no streets gets a metro nobody can reach*; and it never touches freight. Measured on a load of 10,000 in the played mix: 5,590 riders with room to spare, 4,800 with fewer streets, 800 with none, and with the best of everything **the road still carries 39%** of what it would. The road can be halved and it can never be deleted. It is also why the stream split matters to a business: an office and a mill on the same jammed road read 74% and 47% against the road's own 42%, because the mill beats the road by exactly as much of its own traffic as rides the tram, and a lorry in a jam is in a jam. A sector with nothing standing reads the city's own blend rather than a clean road, because the planner costs a first plant at the sector's operating rate and a congested city was cheerfully building plants a 38% road said it could not afford.

**A fare is a price, not a charge.** Nobody chooses to be policed and a patient in a clinic is not shopping; the person on a bus chose to be, and can choose a car instead. So the ridership ceiling is what a *free* system would carry and the fare walks it down on a straight line to nobody at the maximum: free, 5,590 riders; at the default, 5,311; at the ceiling, none. And the two lines move against each other, which is the whole decision — six times the fare takes $58,695 a month instead of $13,276 and puts 1,398 more cars on the road. Jerus asked for a dial that can be made profitable *"by alot"*; it can, at a ridership the city may not want. The fare is money, so a reform moves it — the twenty-third of that family and the first caught in the same edit that created the field — and the ridership curve is written against the cap rather than against dollars, so a reform moves both and nobody changes their mind about the bus. Two things were found on the way: nothing in the infrastructure category had ever had a job, so nobody had written a line to pay one, and a Metro Line is 828 posts; and the fare was charged once a month against a constant that says *a single journey*, so a monthly pass cost $2.50 against a $3,460 wage, seven hundredths of one percent, and the buses could not have paid for themselves at any fare a player would set. That was the transit loss the list had carried as a balance problem. It is 40 journeys a month now — out and back, twenty days — a pass is $100 or 2.9% of an unskilled wage, and the dial stays per ride because that is the number a person on a platform recognises.

> **The fare was collected from nobody**
>
> From the day transit was built until 16 September the city credited itself the fare and debited no household. Nobody saw it because **nothing had ever built a bus**: the playtest's advisor answered every jam with tarmac, so four thousand months a seed, eight seeds a run, not one city ever carried a passenger, and every fixture that needed a road bought a road. The first ensemble in which the advisor bought a Bus Network failed the money audit on all eight seeds, and the residual was the fare to six decimals — 2,186 riders at $2.50 is $5.47, and the audit said 5.465207. *A harness cannot check a thing nobody does.* `MoneyCheck`'s own header says every money bug this codebase has had was a flow with one side, and the twenty-ninth harness could not see this one because its city had no buses. It builds three now. Fixing it found its sibling at once: `setTransit` was missing from the load path, the fifth sighting of that shape, invisible until the fare became real money.

### The railway

Rail is the twelfth sector, and the business that wants to be paid the freight every price in this game has always had inside it. Jerus: *"the freight cant reach zero cause freight needs profit, its its own sector… it wants and will do everything possible to stay profitable and maximize profits. freight money goes to that sector."* There were two ways to write that and only one keeps the audit honest. Paying the railway out of the band would have a payment the books record as going abroad in fact going to a company in the city. So **the band carries only what the lorries still move, and the railway bills the shipper at home**, like any other supplier of a service — the invoice goes on the shipper's input line, where freight belongs in anybody's accounts, the money never leaves the city, and the VAT falls out for free because the ledger already credits a purchase at the supplier's own rate.

```
what a shipper pays a unit  = (1 − share) × baseFreight     // still to the lorries, inside the band
                            + share × quote × baseFreight  // to the railway, on its invoice
allowed  = what a month costs to run + 1.2% of the track it has sunk
quote    = clamp(allowed / what it would bill at the lorry rate × scarcity, 0.30, 1)
```

**A shop's pricing rule cannot price a utility**, and the measurement is what said so. Written first as Retail's shelf — cost plus a quarter — it quoted 32% of the lorry rate, earned $4.5m a month on ten billion of track, and was written down six times: a railway's running cost is a fraction of its capital, so a mark-up on running costs allows a return of nothing on the track. It prices like a regulated network now, running costs plus 1.2% a month on the rate base, floored at 30% of the lorry rate because rail is cheaper than a lorry and not free, capped at one because nobody ships by rail at more than the lorry charges, lifted up to 1.6× by what it cannot carry. It settles at 38–43%. Building too much rail does not make freight cheaper; it makes a railway that cannot pay for itself, and `RailCheck` asserts that a network with four times the track it needs pins at the lorries' price and earns less on four times the capital. The link that falls out of it is real and welcome: **a railway earning 1.2% a month on money that costs it 1% is barely a business, so dear money is what keeps a city's trade band wide**. And the band alone was lying to the sectors: at a 92% quote on 92% of the traffic it said steel's wedge had fallen from 52% to 11% when the shipper had saved eight per cent, because the railway's invoice was not in it. Every place that asks *is this worth exporting* reads a net price now; every place that settles a trade reads the band; with no railway the two are the same number to the bit.

**Track is half a railway.** Capacity is the lesser of the track laid and the wagon sets to run it, at 2,500 tonnes a set and a twenty-year life, so track with no locomotives carries nothing: a Rail Spur is twenty sets, $48m of rolling stock on a $140m spur, and a mature city's million tonnes of track is 420 sets and about 1¾ sets a month of replacement for ever, which is half a Locomotive Works running. Rolling stock is a *pantry* rather than an input — that one line is what makes a bought set accumulate into a fleet instead of vanishing into a month's production — and a save from before trains has trains, because it was hauling, so it had locomotives. The railway will not lay a line under 60% used, Materials' lesson relearned the afternoon a spur went up in a town of four hundred houses and a bank failed over it. It relieves 75% of the bulk it carries off the road, never all of it, because the last mile off a siding is a lorry and a spur reads as 94% trucks; bulk goes before goods, which decides almost nothing today because bulk is 99.7% of the tonnage crossing the boundary. Every tonne it hauls burns $30 of fuel in the world's money, a real import before there is any oil good, so the day `OIL` is a good nothing else changes.

> **What a railway is worth**
>
> Eight seeds, four thousand months each: population **113,178 → 178,975 (+58%)**, GDP **$416.8M → $711.2M a month (+71%)**, per seed 32–91% and 14–113%. On the default seed steel's net wedge goes from 51.6% of the world price to 25.9%. And it is a healthy business in all eight: zero write-downs, zero loss months, the best credit rate in the game, and in seven of eight no debt at all. Three rungs — 50,000, 200,000 and 500,000 tonnes a month at $140m, $520m and $1.24bn — $2,800 of capital per tonne a month on a spur and $2,480 on a terminal, and a terminal nearly three times a Coal Power Plant on the ground, which is the land trade Jerus asked for.

### The vehicles

**Automotive is the thirteenth sector, and it is not for the cars.** Ore becomes steel, steel becomes fabricated steel and machinery, and until 16 September both left, because nothing in the city bought a beam or a machine. An assembly plant is the first thing that does — the fourth link of a chain that stopped at three — and the chain cannot be shortcut: fabricated steel is deliberately not importable, so a city with money and no fabrication shop cannot be in the car business, it can only buy cars. Machinery can come off a ship, at the ceiling its own header had predicted for the day something here bought one, because a car is three and a half tonnes of fabricated steel and four hundred kilos of machinery and the bulky input is the one a city must make. **Cars export; vans and locomotives do not**, from three measurements of one failure: allowed to sell wagon sets to the world, the playtest built **19 Locomotive Works**, 9,880 posts in a city with 25,102 jobs; allowed to sell vans, **240 Commercial Vehicle Plants** shipping 36,000 vans a month; and it was already building 179 Fabrication Works and zero Machine Works. An unbounded export market at a fixed floor means the single best export is built for ever and nothing else ever is; bounded world demand is the general fix and is still its own batch.
