A plant may draw at most a quarter of what the city fabricates, because the first supply gate asked the mills' question — is there spare local supply — and nothing fabricated is ever spare when the world will take all of it; a $172m Assembly Plant sank in month seventeen of a fixture that was measuring tuition, and the harness was right. Eight seeds: GDP $711.2M → $758.8M a month, up in six of eight; seed 0's mature city runs 84 Assembly Plants on 23% of its fabrication.

**The cars are the fourth mode, and the only one that costs.** Highways, transit and rail are all reliefs on an unchanged baseline; a car is the opposite, and it has to be, because the baseline this network always computed was an unmotorised city, unlabelled. It is named now rather than moved:

```
onRoad        = (commuters − riders) × (1 + ownership × (3.0 − 1))     // exactly 1 at zero ownership, to the bit
willingToRide = (1 − ownership) + ownership × 0.75 × jam             // jam is a memory of the commute, a quarter a month
```

Only the people still driving pay it, so a city that motorises *and* builds transit is not charged twice for one journey, and that is what closes Jerus's loop: *"people drive until the road is full, then take the tram."* A car owner rides nothing on a clear morning and three quarters of them ride at a standstill — motorise, nobody rides, it jams, they ride, it clears — read off a memory of the commute rather than last month's road, or it is a two-month oscillator. Transit is a **ceiling on ownership, not a brake on adoption**, and the difference is the whole of whether a player has a move: on the rate it only delays, on the level a well-served city tops out at half a car per household for ever. What motorising costs, eight seeds against the same build with adoption off: **191,194 people and \$848.3M a month at 80% road, against 176,228 and \$695.7M at 73%**, cars in 60% of households and 37% of commuters riding — and the chain is not congestion alone: a worse road costs every new plant at a lower operating rate, marginal projects stop clearing the interest test, business borrowing collapses (\$6.6bn lent against \$18.5bn, the bank at 45% of capacity instead of 77%), Manufacturing's assets fall from \$23.4bn to \$6.3bn, exports fall 26%. A six-point road ratio, compounded over three centuries. `CAR_LOAD_AT_SATURATION = 3.0` is the one constant here that is a game decision rather than a measured one. The advisor learned to buy a bus the same day, and what decides between six candidates is the catalogue: each is costed in trips taken off the road per dollar — a gravel road 900 for \$2,326k against a bus network 2,500 for \$12,000k times the car factor — so a bus loses outright in a city where nobody drives and wins once about half the households own a car. Nobody chose that crossover.

**The vans are the fifth throttle, and the first one a business buys.** Energy, water, road and health all arrive; a lorry is the sector's own capital, sized from a measurement: a city of 106,612 moves 1,169,640 tonnes a month at nameplate, both sides of the door, which at 120 tonnes a vehicle is a fleet of about ten thousand, one commercial vehicle per eleven people, and eighty a month of replacement for ever. Built once without teeth, every ratio in the measured city read 100.0%, because vans are importable and a sector asking for a fleet got one in a month; you cannot put a thousand lorries on the road in a month, so a fleet is built up at an eighth a month and a firm short of its own lorries hires haulage — slowed to 60%, not stopped. Re-measured: 132 sector-months short, worst 65%, every growing sector hitting it and none stopped. A save from before vans owns a fleet, on the railway's own flag: it was moving steel, so it had lorries. And it is what finally gives the Commercial Vehicle Plant a customer.

*What the whole vehicles arc costs a mature city — eight seeds, 4,000 months each*

| Build | Population | GDP a month | Roads |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| No cars, no vans | 191,194 | $848.3M | 80% |
| Cars | 176,228 | $695.7M | 73% |
| Cars and vans | 165,914 | $673.3M | 75% |

About 13% of population and 21% of output against a city where nobody owns anything to move with — for two industries and three decisions it did not have. The households' side of the cars, who buys one and who borrows for it and who sells it last, is in [people](#2-people).

### The instrument panel

Nine batches of transport shipped before any of it was on a screen: the road carried three streams and showed one number, the fare was a real dial with a real elasticity and nothing in the game could turn it, the railway repriced itself every month and told nobody, and a mill running at 65% because it had not taken delivery of its lorries looked exactly like a mill running at 65% for no reason. **Infrastructure** is the twelfth tab on the rail since 0.6.5, after Services because that is where the eye goes looking for it, with four pages that each answer a question somebody actually asks. *Roads*: why is my throughput 73% — the free-flow curve as a banded meter, the three streams as a table with what one trip of each kind costs the street after the highways and the railway have taken their cut, then the cars. *Transit*: the three ceilings and the lowest wins, the two things that walk it down, the books, and the dial. *The railway*: track against the sets that track needs, what it hauls and off which stream, what the rule allows against what it billed, and a box that tells an over-built railway so. *Freight*: the band good by good with what is left of the wedge after rail, the month's bill split into the half billed at home and the half that leaves inside the band, and every sector's fleet — the first time the fifth throttle has been visible anywhere. The fare is the one control, staged like every other policy dial, with a preview that shows riders, fares, net cost and the trips that go back onto the road, and that says plainly what it cannot preview: the second round, where a worse road puts some of them back on the tram. Nothing on the screen builds anything; a second place to buy a building is a second place to maintain. Cars show in both places, on Population beside the household's other assets and on Roads beside the congestion number they explain. The screen shipped without anyone looking at it — the only JavaFX natives here are the Windows build and a Java window cannot be put in the screenshot allowlist — so `InfrastructureCheck` gained a ninth section that walks every accessor the four pages call, in the four city states that break screens, and asks the two questions a renderer cannot survive the wrong answer to: is it finite, and is it inside the range the label claims.

## 21. The screen, time, saves, logs

*The main menu is gone. Twelve destinations sit on a rail down the left — Build, Land office, Population, Services, Infrastructure, Sector economy, Government economy, Finances, The bank, Trade & the world, Policies, Reports — on screen from every screen, with the gear at the foot for anything that leaves the city. A new game opens on* Found a city *since 0.7.10 ([founding a city](#16-founding-a-city)), and a new or loaded city opens on Build, the one screen a player who does not yet know what they are doing can do something on. Pressing a rail button you are already on takes you back to that rail's own front page rather than doing nothing, so there is always a way out of a sub-page without knowing which one you came in by.*

The four red banners became an **inbox**: one live notice per condition, raised from the city's own state rather than restored from a record, carrying this month's figures and one button that goes to the screen that fixes it. A resolved notice gets no button. Since 0.7.8 it says when businesses are going bust and opens the bank's Lending page, and since 0.7.14 the bank's request for preferred shares waits in it with *Answer the bank*, and pauses a running clock if the player has asked the game to pause on events. Services carries a Safety area beside the utilities. The Reports screen plots the city's recorded series, with one heading per group — including *The dead*, which plots the running totals by band since the city was founded, the orphans and the people with no home among them, and the killed — on an axis that is the window rather than forced through zero. The goods page on Reports is thirty-one rows: what a unit costs here this month, the world's band around it, and what crossed the border. There is a palette, fullscreen, keyboard shortcuts, and Resume loads the autosave on a cold start instead of drawing an empty city. Since 0.7.5, on a build page, Enter places every card with a quantity in the page's own order and stops at the first refusal with the rest still pending, and Backspace or Delete takes every quantity back to none (Jerus: *"when you have let's say 3 ready to build, i want to be able to press enter to build"*); the Build button's tooltip says so, a caption under the grid says so while anything is pending, and the Settings screen's list of keys, which had named three, names all six.

**The Reports page was redrawn in 0.7.5.** Jerus: *"two graphs always displayed on the graph rail, the real gdp yearly figure, and the other is the population, and then the third one, the bigger one, the one where you set the stuff, it defaults to the borrowing rate, price level and inflation year on year"*. Two small charts sit at the top, real GDP over the rolling year and the population until the player pins others — a preference that follows the player from city to city and never enters a save; under them the big chart, with the presets, *clear all* and a *log* switch in a row above it, seeded on a first visit with *What money costs*, the city's rate, the price level and inflation. One unit is one real axis as before, two units are two real axes, the second chart laid transparent over the first, and only a third brings back each line squashed to its own range; a crosshair reads every line at the month under the pointer. Recessions are shaded on all three charts, and the year book's episodes are named under the big chart's axis — Jerus's *"little name generator"*: bank equity under zero is a *Financial crisis of 2045*, the rolling year of real output under the year before a *Recession of*, two years of it a *Depression of*, and so on through currency crises, inflations and deflations, epidemics, the treasury under zero and slumps, with runs under three months dropped and runs under six months apart joined (`YearBook.episodes()`), the same lines as the year book's WHAT HAPPENED, so the chart and the file cannot disagree. The picker folds into its groups under a filter box. Since 0.7.6 real GDP can be drawn in its layers ([GDP](#11-tax-policy--gdp)). None of it has been seen on a screen.

The money came onto the screen with it. The strip carries prices and the exchange rate beside the cash since 0.6.10, and the price of money since 0.7.4 ([the currency](#15-prices-the-currency--the-world)). The Money page under Finances is the central bank's balance sheet in the player's words — issued and retired this month, printed since founding, the remittance, what the defence has spent, and M0 and M2 with a year of each. The monetary page under Policies carries the dial and its chips, what the rule would set and where the dial stops, the autopilot, since 0.7.4 the target the rule aims at, the holdings dial, the advances ceiling, the real rate and what savers earn in real terms. The borrow page lists the curve one row per maturity and steps a term loan's chips by ten, and both borrow pages carry the rollover since 0.7.13 and what happens when the bank fails since 0.7.14; the book page says who holds each bond; Finances has the businesses' bond market since 0.7.12 and the city's fund since 0.7.14; and the Trade tab's forces page shows the four terms that move the rate. The Government tab's bridge opens into the treasury's journal and lists the arrears by line, and the bank's desk foots; the Bank tab was rebuilt in 0.7.9 ([the bank](#13-the-bank)). Since 0.7.4 the Sector economy list draws on each card the last 24 months of its net income, green or red on the latest month, with its workers under it, and a *Show more* chip opens every card to revenue, margin, cash, what it owes the bank and posts filled against posts offered — Jerus had asked for *"a little graph of its net income, perhaps how much workers it employs total"*. And the People tab's *EI paid this month* reads what the treasury paid since 0.7.3, after the docs pass found it reading next month's bill, while the People and Summary screens read the care coverage the month actually used rather than one worked out from the beds.

### The interface is a package

Until 18 September every screen was one class: `UserInterface.java`, 25,098 lines, 492 methods, a hundred banner sections, and a session working on the bank had to carry the policy tab's text in the same window. It was nineteen files in `ui/` then and is twenty-one now, with `Ladder` (0.7.6) and `FoundingScreen` (0.7.10), and the model never imports it. `UserInterface` is the window — the stage and its theme, the clock and the speed ladder, the two strips, the rail and the inbox, the save and settings dialogs, the time-skip dialog, the scroller every screen draws into — at about 4,000 lines. Every tab is a class of its own, `BankScreen`, `PolicyScreen`, `PeopleScreen` and so on, its banners moved verbatim with a scripted `ui.` prefix wherever it reaches the window, the Infrastructure tab drawn by `ServicesScreen`, and the left panel's content — the summary, the dashboard, the problem list — is `SummaryScreen`. What every screen shares is four toolkit classes of stateless helpers, `Money`, `Statement`, `Pieces` and `Levers`, reached through an `import static` so that not one of their call sites changed. Twelve model members and two imports were the whole cost of the boundary. The move was mechanical — a dry run prints the couplings and the compiler catches what the script missed — and the one thing the compiler cannot check is the standing rule of this interface: **the month arrives on a clock, so every panel is rebuilt under the player and must restore its own scroll position**. Opening every tab on the split found three small things: the fare dial carried the player to the Policy tab the moment it was let go, because the staged-lever slider redrew the policy screen by name; the Build tab scrolled twice as fast as every other, because it is the one screen whose content sits straight in the page and a wheel floor meant for a notch was raised on every delta of a burst; and the Reports tab moved under the pointer when a line was ticked, because the legend grows a block per line, so that one page keeps its position as pixels from the bottom.

### The statement opens

Jerus: *"can you make it so in the UI when you click on revenue or cogs, it expands and shows the individual items."* One figure that is really ten is a figure a player can read and cannot act on. Four lines on every sector's income statement open now — **Revenue** by good, split city and abroad; the **cost of sales** by good, split city and imported; **Wages** by pay tier, with posts; and **Sales tax remitted**, charged, at the border and credited — and underneath them is a `Sector.Split` per good, booked from the trade rather than reconstructed from units times price, because a local sale and an export clear at different prices in the same month. The first thing it showed was that the city's own bakeries were shipping 62% of what they baked at the world's floor while the shops bought imported meat, fruit and fish by the half-million. A disclosure that discloses nothing is worse than none: a line with one good and nothing shipped does not open, because the caret would promise a breakdown and then repeat the figure above it — and the rule about how many rows there are has to count the rows, since Construction sells no goods at all and fell straight through a rule about goods to draw a caret onto one row that repeated its total. That *other revenue* turned out to be two businesses under one label, work recognised off the order book and this month's repairs billed to every standing building, and a city whose building work has stopped and whose repair income is still growing is a city that has finished growing. The parts are frozen into the statement when it is struck, like the per-good money, because a screen reading a working field late describes a month the statement above it is not about.

The same disclosure reached two more statements on 19 September. The Government tab's bridge from the budget to the treasury's cash opens its last row into the treasury's journal, with what the journal cannot explain printed under it as *Not accounted for* ([tax, policy and GDP](#11-tax-policy--gdp)); and the bank's trading desk, whose opened lines had never added up to its total because the re-mark was left out, foots ([the owners and the exchange](#9-the-owners-the-bonds--the-exchange)). A row with nothing to disclose stays a plain row. Because the panel is rebuilt every month under the player, a line drawn closed every time snapped shut each month while the player was reading it; since 0.7.9 a screen can keep a set of the lines it has open (`Statement.opens()`), and the Bank tab is the one that does — every other screen's opened lines still snap shut, which is on the list.

### Time runs on its own

There is no *next month* button. The city runs on a clock at five seconds a month (`SECONDS_PER_MONTH`) and a speed the player picks off a snapping ladder — 0.1× · 0.25× · 0.5× · 1× · 2× · 5× · 10× · 20× · 50× — with the space bar as play/pause and the arrow keys moving the ladder. The day inside the month is painted so the city looks alive between the ticks, even though nothing in the model moves until the month turns.

Three things that only matter once the month arrives unasked. A frame that takes a long time is **clamped at a quarter second**, so a stalled window cannot swallow thirty months while it was away — the worst a single frame can advance is 2.5 months. Redraw is capped at one in every 120ms, because at 50× a month lands every 100ms and the screen cannot usefully be redrawn faster than it can be read. And a panel is now rebuilt *while the player is still looking at it*, so every scrolling page has to hold its own position across the rebuild rather than snapping to the top — which took seven attempts and a trace file to get right, and is written up on its own.

The game can pause itself when something happens, and by default it does not: the setting exists, and it is off, because a clock that stops without being asked is worse than a notice that waits.

### The summary is a problem list

The summary panel used to be six fixed rows — economy, tax, labour, health, land, people. Of the sixteen problems a player can actually build their way out of it could show exactly one, health, and only as a sick rate. A city with no water, no cells and nowhere to bury its dead read exactly like a city with none of those problems.

It is two lists now. **NEEDS YOU** carries twenty conditions that have a lever, yellow near the line and red past it, each row a door to the screen that owns the fix, and each disappearing when it is solved; when it is empty it names the condition closest to its yellow line instead, so it is never blank. **HOW THE CITY IS** carries seven readings with no dial — out of work, off sick, hungry, people a month, doubled up, ground used, the currency — always present, coloured when bad, and its door goes to the screen that *diagnoses* rather than the one that fixes.

Writing it turned up a model bug that no harness had: `getEnergyRatio()` and `getWaterRatio()` both return min(supply / demand, 1), so a row keyed off them could not appear until the lights were already out. They read load — demand over supply — now, against the 75% the dashboard has called "tight" all along.

### The calendar

Month 1 is January 2000. Purely presentational, with deliberately no reverse function — nothing should derive a month from a date string.

### Skipping time

A skip takes a snapshot before, samples *every month* during, and diffs a snapshot after. Episodes cannot be reconstructed from endpoints: a city that starved for fifty months and recovered looks identical at both ends to one that never had a problem. The report counts months short of power, water, land and road capacity, months nothing was built, epidemics and their worst month, and the peak unburied — then writes plain sentences ordered by how much each should worry you. Since 0.7.8 it says what lenders wrote off, amber only past a sound book's loss, and since 0.7.15 a skip no longer stops at an empty treasury: it stops only when a month throws, and says what the central bank advanced over it and what is owed at the end.

### Saves

Ten numbered slots plus an autosave, under `%APPDATA%` on Windows and the platform equivalent elsewhere — chosen because Steam Cloud syncs from known roots and a bare home folder is not one. Writes go to a temp file, back up the existing save, then atomically move; the worst case is a stray temp file and a save one autosave old. History graphs are per slot. Autosave fires every twelve months, before any skip, and on quit.

The save format is at **27**, and its changelog is the best history the project has. Older saves load, back to format 21; what is refused is a save from a newer build and one from before the sector template. Nineteen carried the household balance sheet, twenty the repriced unit of material — an old yard read at its old value — and twenty-one the sector template, which was a clean break. Twenty-two was business services, twenty-three manufacturing, twenty-four the farms, twenty-five the bank's own cost of funds, twenty-six the price index's water-marks and **twenty-seven the sixth age band** — which also made every band-indexed array save its band *names* beside its values, so the day a seventh band arrives no existing file is read at the wrong offsets. The thirteen foods went in *without* a bump, because goods have been saved by name since the sector template: a good this build does not know is dropped and says so in the log, which is what happens to an old city's warehouse of `FOOD`. And so did everything the batches of the edition before this one added — five sectors, the freight band, the three streams, the modes and the fare, the railway's quote and its locomotives, every sector's fleet, the households' cars, their investment income, the luxury baseline and the dinners they ate — because a sector is keyed by name, a market is keyed by name, and every new figure in a household cell is appended to the end of an array whose reader checks its length. A city saved before them opened with no cars, no fleets, no kitchens, and the rolling stock its track implies, which is exactly what that city was; an eleven-sector build was proved to load a ten-sector save to the cent before the first of the five shipped. **The central bank went in without a bump too**, and so did everything around it: the treasury's journal for both months and its raised counter; the two health dials, the coverage each month used and a cell slot for the share of a cell's people who could pay for care; the grant's basis and amount, the loan's rate and the tuition scale on the policy array's tail; the vault in dollars and its revaluation (slots 22 and 23 of the foreign accounts), the debt's revaluation (24), the defence (25–27) and the real rate differential with its two inflations (28–30); what the bank still owes for paper sold between the presses, under two keys; the central bank's books, the arrears, the autopilot, the policy rate boxed so that a 0% dial reloads at 0%, the holdings dial and the advances ceiling, each under its own key; who holds every bond, saved with the bond; the households' paper as the thirty-first slot of a cell, with its book ratio; and a buyback's holders outside the pools. The fold and the spend factor added nothing: the first is a rule about counts, and the second is struck again on load. A city saved by 0.6.7 opened in 0.7.3 with an empty central bank, the vault it had bought if it bought one, the bank holding all of its paper and nothing in arrears — exactly what that city was — and a city saved by 0.7.2 pays one month's EI twice on its first month, once. Between them the long sick, the people outside the families, the household record and the whole crime system went in *without* a bump, deliberately: Gson leaves a missing key alone, and a format-21 city loads with each of them empty, which is correct for that city. A big saved city comes back with only its founding constabulary and shows the crime notice until it builds a station.

**And everything since went in without a bump as well**, each batch's new figures under keys of their own or on the end of an array whose reader knows its older widths: the inflation target's key, the three tax bases and then a tuition scale for each of the nine kinds of school on the policy array's tail, each school kind's month on the end of the schools' array; the history's new series — two a sector, GDP's four parts, the dial, the bank's prime, deposit rate and fees, and six of its capital — with an older history's strain premium skipped on load; the land office's choice of how to pay, its listing behind a marker that says its prices are dollars, the office's dollar ground price as a fourth slot, and the land's dollars as slots 31–36 of the foreign accounts; the bank's pricing record and its late profit, its allowance, its capital record, its month's lines and a year of them, its year of balance sheets and its equity's two parts; every borrower's last quarter, the builders' salvage and a statement's stock paid for earlier; the households' account fee on the end of their statement; the eight keys of the founding record; the mortgages, saved among the business debts under their own type with the insurance's three counters and two lines on the government's month; the bond market, each cell's bonds as the thirty-second slot and bond by bond by name, the exchange's books, and the interim loans under a type of their own; the rollover's setting, ledger and record; the city's fund, the bank's preferred and its record, three slots a company on the register for the city's holdings and a city holder on every bond, and the four inputs the debt market's rate was struck from; and what the central bank has paid the households for their paper and paid at issue rolling its own. The pins on the Reports page are a preference in `settings.json`, not the city's. A city saved by the build the last edition described opens in this one as exactly the city it was: aiming at 2% and taxing profit, sales and wages at one rate, charging every school one price, its listed land read as dollars at the rate of the day it is loaded, its bank's pricing record refilling a month at a time and its allowance set up on load from the book it carried, founded as Danzik in the Danzik dollar on D\$2.5B and US\$1B, with no mortgages, no bonds, no fund and no preferred, the rescue on the button, nothing rolled and its dial on whichever hand it was saved with. A holdings dial past half, saved by this build and opened in an older one, is held at half.

### Logs

Every `println` in the game already goes to a rotating log file, because a logging system that needs a thousand edits does not get adopted. In a packaged build there is no console, so all of it previously went nowhere. Reports and graphs to the log default off, so the 2 MB log holds the crash rather than three centuries of ASCII graphs.

## 22. How it's checked

*Sixty-four self-hosted harnesses plus a 4,002-month playtest that audits every month, asserts money is conserved to the cent, and reloads the city repeatedly to prove a saved game and a played one agree. `AllChecks` runs all sixty-five, one JVM each, in about four and a half minutes — 263 seconds on 28 September, in a cloud session where the one that needs JavaFX, `BuildMenuCheck`, is skipped: sixty-three green and one red, `HealthCheck`. Its red line reads the hunger of a city charging fifteen times the founding fees for care against a free one's over their last year, and since partway through 0.7.12 the dear city has been hungrier by more than the price of care — 8.4 points against a tolerance of five on 28 September ([health](#4-health)); it shipped red on Jerus's word,* "Ship with it red, flagged"*, and has a batch of its own on the list. The line that stood here before, `InfrastructureCheck`'s* "and its shops can actually be supplied"*, which Jerus put down to roads —* "its fine, we will balance later." *— went green by accident on one build of 0.7.2 and red again on the next, and has passed on every suite since 0.7.7; the fixture is sensitive to the young city's rates, so it stays on the list. Every count and constant on this page is struck from the tree at 0.7.15; every measurement carries its date or its batch, and "the default seed on 28 September" is the plain playtest run that night. `RealismCheck`, a probe outside the build, is the rebalance's instrument and the thing to run first if any real-world figure is questioned. And since 18 September the playtest is the gate for a refactor as well as for a mechanic: it is deterministic, two baseline runs are byte-identical, and every move out of `Game` and every comment-only pass was proved by a run that compared equal to the morning's, bar its wall-clock line.*

| Harness | Asserts |
| --- | --- |
| MoneyCheck | a prospering city and a broke, banned, taxed, importing one both conserve money to $0.00 — every dollar that leaves a pool arrives in another or crosses the border in a way the audit can name. Closing this identity found four leaks nothing else had seen, and it is what caught theft leaving the tills; since 0.7.6 land paid for out of the vault moves nothing the audit cannot see |
| ConservationCheck | nothing was created or destroyed — food in equals food out plus the change in stock, exactly, with no slack; electricity revenue equals what was charged; three consecutive loads into the *same* object |
| SectorBooksCheck · BooksCheck · TreasuryCheck | every sector's statement foots under one template, and every opened line adds up to the line above it, the home and abroad halves reached by a different route from the totals the VAT is struck off; every sector's operations page — 17,219 screen lines a run — reads as a figure and never as a sentinel, an infinity or a NaN, because the Agriculture screen once printed $9,223,372,036,854,775,807 in red; the government's books date to the month they happened; maintenance is an operating cost and reaches the builders as an order; the treasury's bridge foots through its journal, land and a building stay on the budget's own line and are not named twice, and what nothing explains is the first coupon's timing to the cent — net, since 0.7.3, of the coupons the households and the central bank were paid the same month, which a founding bank quoting its savers 7,567% had hidden; and since 0.7.13 the rollover's arithmetic on the brief's own figures — a city in surplus with two notes falling due in a row, one that built this year and rolls everything, and a surplus city's dollar note rolled abroad in dollars |
| EquityCheck · ExchangeCheck | shares issued equal shares held; a dividend leaves a till and arrives in a household; and since 0.7.12, on the book: the price is the last trade, nobody is obliged to trade, the desk keeps to its two caps and offers what is over them at fair value, the leavers, the world and each household cell post by their own rules and cell trades with cell, a buyback's unspent money stays in the company, a split does not move anybody's wealth, and the register and the books survive a reload and a live city |
| BondCheck · OrderBookCheck | a bond is at par at its own coupon and its price falls as the yield rises; bookbuilding sets the coupon at the lowest yield that fills the issue and the rest is a bank loan; a small amount goes to the bank and a large one to a bond, and where they cross; each participant posts by its own rule, a company never bids for its own bonds, and the world's purchase crosses the border; a slice takes a loan's loss off the loans and a bond's off the bonds, and the bondholders' loss reaches every class; concentration costs Basel's capital, rising with a sector's share and falling as the book spreads; at maturity every holder is paid its face; and the book itself — the best price first and at one price the first to come, a trade at the resting order's price, nobody obliged, partial fills, no trade with oneself, a buyer short of cash and a seller short of the thing, a reform, and a save with every resting order in its place |
| LabourCheck · EducationCheck | every wage equals its PayTier at the default floor, so the old balance is provably intact; no band staffs more posts than it has people; a doctor shortage is priced on doctors; the wage index walks to the published price index a twenty-fourth a month through 240 months of inflation, a reform and a reload; nobody graduates before the course is over and somebody does once it is; each of the grant's four bases pays what it says, a loan at 5% costs a graduate exactly its interest and a prisoner nothing, and a tripled fee brings the trap back; and since 0.7.6 one school's price moves only its own fee, the every-school setter moves all nine, and after a load the nine charge nine prices |
| BankCheck | what to pay savers is the bank's decision, and one whose margin is gone pays them nothing; since 0.7.7 a strained bank quotes what an unstrained one with the same costs does, a new loan's rate is its four parts and is fixed for its term, a flush bank passes on less of the dial than one at the window, the fees reach the bank to the cent, the window is the dial and a quarter point, and the owners are paid on what the tax leaves; the bank pays for the city's paper at the settle, and the section fails four ways on the old order; the desk's statement foots; since 0.7.8 a reload reads the same month, a loan is met by its year's allowance and a write-off by the allowance first, a bank that has lived through a bad year chooses more capital, under its target it keeps its profit and lends slower, inside its band it pays a share of its profit, while it stands there is always something it will lend, capital is the constraint and can run out, the default curve takes a sector's slice pro rata and the backstop writes down only a sector with nothing left, the allowance is staged firm by firm, the audit closes through months of slices, a failing sector's plant goes to the builders as material, the bank reads a borrower on its last quarter, and its buybacks and its desk keep to its spare capital; and the Bank tab's arithmetic — the ladder's parts are prime at every dial, the weight table foots, the balance sheet foots this month and a year ago, and paid-in, retained and the city's preferred add up to equity to the cent every month |
| CreditCheck · MortgageCheck | a business loan is prime plus the borrower's own expected loss off the curve, and pays its fee out of its proceeds; its rate is fixed at issue; lending stops at the borrower's own default point with the ceiling a real gap below it, a shut lender lends nothing, a repeat defaulter is shut out for longer and one ban stops the investment advisor too; the quote is the deal, and a note raises what it was asked to; and since 0.7.12 nothing is lent past the default point, read on the quarter, a month that cannot pay defaults and what is still unpaid is lent as interim financing ranked first, a rationing bank covers a short month and refuses growth, and a new sector's month-ends of nothing are not a quarter. A mortgage is a level annuity with nothing left at the end; the landlord's own funds and the premium on top; a landlord short of its down payment holds, and says so; the lender's test passes at its line and not a hair under; the rate is fixed for its term and the rent floor reads its interest and not its principal; an insured slice is paid to the bank by the city; the bank weighs it at nothing and prices it with no loss; the leverage ratio holds capital against its face; a branch that does not pay is closed after its fuse and never the last; and a dividend is paid after principal |
| ForeignCheck · ForeignDebtCheck · CapitalFlowCheck · MonetaryCheck · DenominationCheck | the books balance over ten years of foreign servicing to 5e-14 and the bank bought none of it; the vault is the founders' dollars less what the defence sold, held in dollars through a fall; since 0.7.6 land bought by converting pushes the rate exactly as buying the same reserves would, which is not at all; original sin feeds its own premium; the world's curve values a dollar bond by its months left; a run needs fragility and a shock; the Taylor principle holds, and since 0.7.4 a 0% and a 5% target differ by exactly `TAYLOR_WEIGHT` × 5 points and the target stops at 20%; inflation falls with the rate, 1.304 points from a 3% dial to a 40% one on 28 September; a reform is bit-exact and a reformed city reloads as itself, with every opened statement line divided along with its total and the desk's room in every company — which is shares — left exactly alone |
| CentralBankCheck | money made less money destroyed is the change in M0, in a month with every kind of flow in it and in every month of a played city; the bank earns exactly the dial on its reserves and pays the window its penalty over it, a quarter point since 0.7.7; a debt-free note prices at the dial; a broke treasury draws advances and repays them first; past the ceiling the promises are paid and the rest owed, and paid down first when cash returns; the rule moves the dial and the player's hand stops it; the holdings dial buys the bank's term paper with money it makes, bends the long end by exactly the compression and never the note, sells back within the speed's months and keeps its pace across a save; the ceiling is the player's dial; a reform scales the money and not the ratios; and since 0.7.15 the dial takes the whole of the paper with the compression whole from half, the city's floor is split by who holds the paper, what it holds of a maturing piece it takes again at issue par for par, and last year's surplus pays the market's part first |
| HoldersCheck | at the settle the households take their share and the bank the rest; each coupon reaches each holder in its share; a household short of money sells its paper before its shares, and below face after a hike; a buyback pays every holder, and a dollar bond bought back is money leaving the country — the section fails with a residual when its audit line is deleted; a save from before the holders loads with the bank holding everything; and at the whole of the paper the central bank buys the households' once the bank's is gone |
| FundCheck | a failed bank is resolved for its shares the month it fails, or frozen and carrying its hole until the button is pressed; the bank's new shares go to others and the city's stake falls; the preferred is on TARP's terms and is repaid at its third anniversary from capital over target and then from new shares; the offer comes through the inbox, again a quarter after a decline, and through a save; the dial takes its share of the year's surplus, keeps the floor and uses the surplus once; the rule keeps 70/30, its 10% limit and its band, and cash that does not fit waits; the 3% transfer is a twelfth a month, from cash only; the hand trades at fair value, and paying in and drawing out stay off the budget; every piece survives a save; and Insane is founded with nothing and its ground owed abroad, and never borrowing, plays on the central bank's advances |
| CurrencyCheck | the real rate moves the currency and the inflation differential does not — ten months of 40% inflation with no outflow move it by the parity pull alone; the defence sells the vault's capacity times the month's deficit to the cent and damps by what it sold, and an empty vault damps nothing; what the dollars fetch is the central bank's equity, not money destroyed, and M0 does not move; the dial, the rule and the appetite are uncapped; past 100 the rate goes where the push takes it, and a reform scales the guards |
| PopulationCheck · HouseholdCheck · HouseholdMemoryCheck | the city fills toward its jobs, keeps taking arrivals while crowded, and sheds people only after a tier has been dying a year; every band-indexed array is saved with its band names and the legacy list of five is pinned as five, so that nobody ever "tidies" it into tracking the enum; all seventy-eight ledgers balance and survive a save by name, and a pensioner in one band draws what a pensioner in the other does; an emptied cell folds all seven of its stocks to the cent; the spending factor is exactly one less the saving response times the real deposit rate on everything above subsistence, and subsistence does not move; the rebuild keeps what it can and re-forms the rest |
| HealthCheck · SicknessCheck · DeathRecordCheck | the workforce, wage bill and payroll do not move while output falls; outbreaks fire, decay and end; graves and backlogs survive a reload; the ring of the long sick kills at the right rate and clinics stop it; the fee scale reaches the three care fees and not the funerals, a household that cannot pay goes without care and not without food, a rich city is served exactly as before, and the premium lands to the penny; every death is attributed to a band and the running totals carry across a gap; and, read over its last year since 0.7.12, that a dear-care city is no hungrier than a free one by more than the price of care, which is the line that is red |
| OutsideCheck | the labour-pool identity holds to a person; a claim runs exactly twelve months, and is paid in the month it is credited; a student is out of the supply and repays after; closing the biggest employer puts its people on EI, paid the month it is credited; a row past EI that cannot pay its rent is evicted by the share unpaid, and a quarter of the evicted leave |
| CrimeCheck | K reproduces Canada's rate at Canada's coverage; every cell of the pressure table; more police is always less crime and never none; the six-month ring, a full prison and an early release; the crime pull on migration; and a bare city at 2.4× Canada's rate against a policed twin at 0.16× |
| ConsumptionCheck | the two laws across the whole income range rather than at a point; that a household off the end of the curve still eats; that a famine diet scores worse than a mixed one; that the same file at a hundred times the prices buys the same food to the gram; that the enum's thirteen prices and the data file's agree to the cent; and that the city's money and the world's are never divided into one another by accident |
| BusinessServicesCheck · ManufacturingCheck · AgricultureCheck | one per sector since the template, and each asserts the thing that sector alone can get wrong: an office refuses to open without licensed engineers and opens with them; steel clears between the mills' floor and the import ceiling once something here buys it, and the mills book a local sale for the first time; the relief reaches the land half of a field's assessment and not its barns, and a farm's worth is stated in money at the world's floor, because four farms in two units cannot share a tonnage column |
| FoodProcessingCheck | all three plants are reachable by the sector's own planner where the generic one would have seen one; a first plant is valued with its own nameplate in the supply rather than at the ceiling it will destroy; twenty points on the sales tax moves what a plant is thought to earn; meat at a farm's floor is worth more to a Meat Works than meat off a ship and the difference is most of what the works is worth; and the fixture runs until the sector is about to build rather than for a number of months, holding the sector so the state under test is reached by construction |
| TradeCostCheck · RailCheck | not one delivered price moved and freight is three quarters of the half-wedge, against a table of what the prices were that morning; every building's three loads add to its road load to the bit and the network's total is the sweep it always was; the road can be halved and never deleted; a jammed city with good transit keeps its offices working and its lorries in the jam; free transit carries the ceiling, the default fare nearly all of it, the ceiling fare nobody, and a month of riding is a share of a wage somebody would recognise; a city with no railway is the city it was to the bit on all four prices, what leaves the band plus what the railway bills is the blended rate over twenty-five pairs, every dollar of haulage is on a shipper's cost line, track with no trains carries nothing, and four times the track it needs cannot be charged for |
| CarCheck · VanCheck | a city with nobody driving is the city it was, and the factor is one exactly; a fully motorised city asks three of the road; at a standstill three quarters of the owners are on the tram and one good month does not empty it; a month of car sales is real money and the savings really left; no household owns less than none of a car or more than one; a household short of the cash still buys, on credit, the seller is paid in full and a lender found the difference; a family that cannot feed itself puts the car up and somebody buys it, and a city where everybody is selling gets the floor and nothing else; a metro built after the cars unmotorises the city to its ceiling; a sector's fleet is sized by what its plant moves, both ways through the door, one with none is slowed to the floor and not stopped, a fleet is built up at an eighth a month and wears out in ten years, and a save from before vans reads as a sector that has never been asked |
| RestaurantsCheck | a meal is a ninetieth of a person-month in both directions; empty tables charge the floor, a full kitchen the middle, a queue near the ceiling, monotone between them, and a Diner clears its wages at half its tables after the sales tax; ninety dinners feed one of a couple and a hundred and eighty feed the household, at a hundred times the price exactly the same, and a dinner is eaten once; a city that could buy anything still eats a third of its meals out; the kitchens restock off every one of the thirteen in the basket's proportions; and a queue at a door that is not there is a reason to build one |
| YearBookCheck · HistoryCheck | the year book folds each series the way that series has to be folded — a flow sums, a level takes December, a rate averages and keeps its worst month — and the file says so; a decimal point survives a French locale; and the unemployment column is the model's own rate on a played city that has somebody studying, because a harness that only checks the arithmetic will certify the wrong number; since 0.7.5 the named episodes — a history with the bank under water for fourteen months and output that loses fourteen dollars for good gets exactly two names and exactly the shading, a two-month failure names nothing, and two failures in one year are "…, again" six months apart and one crisis five months apart. Every series is recorded every month and survives a save, each sector's two since 0.7.4, GDP's four parts adding to the month's GDP since 0.7.6, the dial and the bank's prices and capital since 0.7.7 and 0.7.8; and a history from before the premium went still loads |
| StaleCheck | the prose still describes the code: `tools.Stale` reads the tree and `docs/` and finds a javadoc with no member under it, prose naming a source file or a page that is not there, and a stated count of banners, harnesses or interface files that is out; a fixture with three planted lies has each one come back, a sound file has none, and the tree itself is at zero on all three — it shipped red on purpose, with 84 orphaned javadocs across 40 files, all real and all older than the tool |
| NewGameCheck · LandCheck | a city that never existed, a new one after a load, and one that is actually playable; since 0.7.10 the founding record, the starts and their bounds, a currency per city, an old save as Danzik, and the build screen's twenty-year bond sized to the gap at every maturity with the plant built and the audit closing; since 0.7.13 the dial and the rollover a new game founds with. The land office's allocation, listing and floor, a tract that can hold a mining district, and the price as a density policy; since 0.7.6 a price in dollars paid at the day's rate, converting and paying from the vault each closing its month, a short vault converting the rest and an older listing read as dollars; since 0.7.13 square kilometres, and a funding page sized to the gap for one plot or several, with no dollar offer while the window abroad is shut |
| SaveFileCheck · ReadPathCheck · BuildingDataCheck | a played city and a reloaded one agree figure for figure, and since 0.7.14 the fund, its rescue setting and the bank's preferred with them; a freshly loaded city's first read is what the live one reads; `buildings.json` produces exactly the built-in definitions, field by field |
| …and fifteen more | build menu, calendar, the carry trade, GDP, housing, the inbox, infrastructure, investment, mining, policy, restructuring, robustness, save slots, skip reports, water |

> **Rules the harnesses are written to**
>
> **A fixture must cause the condition, not wait for it. Assert against the model's own constants, never a literal** — a check pinned to 0.06 or 2.25 tests that nobody edited the harness. **Assert the shape of a distribution, not only its total** — an aggregate cannot see a missing category. **Count how often a new mechanic actually fires in a real run** — out-migration once shipped fully tested and fired zero times in 4,002 months, and foreign borrowing had to be told to happen. **A quantity in one unit tested against a rule that assumed another** is the shape that keeps recurring. **A fixture has to cause the condition under test, not stand next to it** — fifty-odd sightings now, the latest a fixture that measured an oven's revenue on one of its two products and reported it losing money. **When a fix is safe because some case is exactly unchanged, assert that case at zero tolerance** — a sector making one good must carry exactly 1.0 of its own cost, and that is a check rather than a comment. **A harness cannot check a thing nobody does** — the fare was collected from nobody for as long as no fixture had built a bus. **When a harness goes red on your change, ask the same question of ten fixtures before believing it is your change** — one fixture said the farms broke the currency reform; ten said the model had been carrying a coin-toss for months. **A sentinel is a value for the code to compare, never a value to print**, and the place it leaks is the screen, which was the one layer with no harness behind it — and the plainer rule beside it: play the game, because fifty-one green harnesses and a ten-fixture sweep did not find a nine-quintillion-dollar unit cost that clicking on Agriculture found in ninety seconds. **Assert the premise the whole suite stands on** — a `month++` left twice at the top of the month passed every harness in the suite, and only the playtest's month numbers gave it away; `CalendarCheck` asserts one press is one month now. **Is the field money? Then it belongs in the reform the day it is written** — a rule cheaper than the twenty-five constants of the family before it. **A held sector is held in both directions** — a planner that could demolish a harness's fixture scrapped six spurs of an over-built railway, and an assertion whose subject is decided by a planner is an assertion about the planner. **A fixture says what it lives on** — when the founding treasury went from D\$2.5B to D\$100M, forty-two fixtures in twenty-five harnesses turned out to have been living on it, only ten went red, and three were green because their calendars had quietly run short; each is handed its treasury explicitly now (0.7.10). **Compare mechanisms, not counts** — a last-bit rounding difference moves an eight-seed count of bank failures by about three and the amount written off by about \$60bn (0.7.8).

> **Decided by dust**
>
> The money-constant family — a bound written in absolute money that a currency reform walks past — is past twenty-five sightings, and since 16 September it has two relatives that are not constants at all. **The sign of a residue.** Four retired households owed minus 2.7e-29 dollars, out of the monthly rebuild handing a cell `weight × g / g`, which can come back an ulp above `weight`. The magnitude is not money and nothing reads it as money; one thing reads its *sign* — `investAbroad()` asks `debt <= 0` to decide who may keep money abroad — so four cells flipped, their paper came home at a tenth a month, the financial account moved by thousands, and the exchange rate, which is every import and export price in the city, moved with it: a city and its reformed twin ran together at 1e-13 for 158 months and were 2–4% apart a decade later. The fix is four clamps and no numbers, because a ratio cannot go stale in a new unit. *A zero-crossing test is a threshold, and a threshold on a residue is decided by luck.* **A money ratio that comes out as a physical quantity.** The car affordability test is money over money and the answer is cars, which the road, the market and the trade balance all read; `(a/100)/(b/100)` is not `a/b`, so a reformed city wanted an ulp more of a car, bought it somewhere else, and `DenominationCheck` went red on sixteen assertions. Scale-invariant in arithmetic and not in floating point, and the cure is a grain: a cell buys whole cars, and the shops sell whole baskets. The playtest flags any household position below zero at zero tolerance, every month of every seed, and was seen to fail 216 times before it was trusted.
>
> Two more sightings since. **A hair of borrowing is a discrete state** (0.6.8): the waterfall clamps a negative remainder, but a positive 1e-21 becomes a debt, and `investAbroad()` gates on `debt <= 0`; the first draft of the price at the door re-split a row's bill by its paying heads, and the reform twins parted a decade later over *interest 2.36e-21 against 0.0* in one cell. The re-split was dropped rather than touch the waterfall. **A ghost household** (0.7.2): a cell whose census count had fallen to a residue — 1e-15 households, or a real 0.3 — still held savings and was still being paid, a household to some lines and not to others, and one line divided a credit by it; `DenominationCheck` went red at a floating-point knife-edge and the trace found it. The cure is a grain again: under half a household a cell is empty, and `DenominationCheck` looks 202 times over both cities and finds no cell under half a household holding anything. And one in the harness itself: its own two dust thresholds were fixed dollar amounts until 0.7.12, and scale with the currency now.

### The tree, and the prose that describes it

The tree is 226 files and 177,379 lines: one flat package plus `sectors/`, `ui/` and `tools/`. `Game.java` is the seam every system meets at, 12,363 lines and thirty-four banner sections, and on 18 September four mechanics that already had the shape of a class left it with their text intact and their behaviour byte-for-byte unchanged — the households' car market as `Motoring`, the boutiques and the kitchens as `LuxuryCounter`, who is at risk of offending as `Offending`, what the city eats as `CityBasket` — each called from the same line of the month it always was, with every moved getter kept on `Game` as a delegation so that no caller changed. The currency reform stayed, because it redenominates twenty-two subsystems through `Game`'s own fields and that is the seam doing the seam's job. The investor, the foreign borrowing and demographics are bigger and entangled, and each would be a plan of its own.

Nobody reads those files whole. `tools/` reads the sources as text and writes `docs/`: a code map with one row per file and one page per file listing its banners and every method with its line; `dials.md`, every `static final` with its value and the sentence above it, 997 of them; `month-order.md`, the month as a numbered list of statements with where each call goes, which is what section 01 of this page is struck against; and `harnesses.md`, the 5,807 labelled assertions under their sections and which harnesses name which class — which is how it is known that nothing yet names `Automotive` or `LuxuryRetail`. `Where` finds a member or a banner by name and prints it; `SaveDump` looks inside a save without loading it. And every batch has a sixth step since 18 September, done by a context that did not make the change: a docs pass that makes every comment, header, index and count agree with the code again, because the agent that changed the code has stopped seeing the prose. Its first run found four stranded javadocs and two false headers; its mechanical half is `tools.Stale`, which found 84 orphaned javadocs on its first run and is at zero now; the half that needs judgement stays with a reader, and four comments whose numbers disagreed with their constants were decided by Jerus — *"the code is correct, the comments are the outliers."*

## 23. Open questions

*Known, measured, and written down rather than discovered later. These are decisions, not defects. Thirty-four stood here in the last edition. Four have been answered since, eleven have moved and are rewritten, and the twelve batches from 0.7.4 to 0.7.15 opened thirteen more — forty-three, reconciled against the project's own list on 28 September.*

| Question | What is measured |
| --- | --- |
| The city's size is hypersensitive to a small steady drag | Seven *hundredths* of a point added to the sick rate, with no crime at all, ends two seeds **9% smaller**; at a thousandth of crime's strength another ends 16% smaller. It predates every recent batch, and it means an eight-seed median can hide or invent a 10% effect. **The first thing to look at next.** |
| A bank with no lending business | **Half answered, and the other half closed by measurement.** On the default seed on 22 September the bank lends $13.2bn of $77.9bn deposited and runs at 69% of its capacity, and on 28 September it ended with $131M lent of $293bn deposited, at 13%. Since 0.7.0 its spare cash earns the policy rate at the central bank rather than the world's 2% abroad, which changes what idle money pays and not how much of it there is. Nothing borrows below what the money costs the lender now, and over sixteen seeds failures went 5.0 → 0.0 median, recapitalisation $3.8bn → $0, months run at a loss 44–58% → 3–14%. The intended next step — a real intermediary funding domestic investment out of domestic savings — was measured and dropped: the bank lends **1.87% of its deposits** at home and runs at 31–49% of the capacity it already has. The city's savings are on the order of two hundred thousand times what its productive sector wants to borrow. It is demand-limited, not funding-limited, and deposit-gathering cannot change that. The open question is what a city this rich should be able to *do* with the money. |
| Cities that empty out, and nothing notices | Over sixteen seeds, nine had a population drawdown of more than half — median worst 57%, deepest 77% — and it is present in the control build too, so it is not new. Every one of those runs reports "Nothing. Every month passed the audit." The money conserves, the books foot, and a city loses three people in four with no finding raised. **The audit has no measure of a city shrinking**, nor of one running away the other way: on a Lean founding in 0.7.13, seed 0 ended owing $476.6T with 43.9% of its people out of work, and the playtest raised no finding. |
| Savings that cannot be spent | Read off a real screen, slot 3, month 2305, a city of 1,003,081. The 1,361 households in *out of work, EI run out* are each \$390 a month short, have **\$201,363 put by** — 516 months of cover — and have defaulted. **The reading is settled and the fix is not made**: the draw-down path is wired, and the discharge fires anyway because `discharge()` tests the *wage* against subsistence and never looks at savings — a bug in the opposite direction, and why a city with no poor people in it manufactures bankruptcies. It belongs with the supply work. Alongside it: orphan bands three orders of magnitude apart on a 2,300-month steady state. The prisoners' \$70 student loan that stood here was the balance they carried in — nothing collects a student loan except from a working family — and since 0.6.9 the freeze is the prisoner's own, no instalment and no interest. |
| The index's base period | The basket is weighted from a month two years in, and the shelf-price row below says the shelf floor holds the level at about 0.78 and it cannot fall further — so a run reading near that has been measured partly against a floor rather than against its own start. A rebased version is built and not shipped: `DeathRecordCheck` goes red on it with the orphan count moving the other way (60→73 as shipped against 59→46 rebased), which is a directional flip and wants explaining before either number is trusted. |
| The landlock predicate does not clear | `Game.isPrivateInvestmentLandLocked()` reads true at month 12 with 1,974,000 sq ft still free, and is still true at month 300. `landBlockedSectors` does not appear to be emptied, so the inbox notice "your businesses have nowhere to build" is very likely firing on cities with plenty of ground. The summary deliberately does not use it. |
| The households' trillion | **Half answered, and the half that is left is a supply question.** The hoard was diagnosed on 17 September — foreign coupons compounding abroad at 1.58% a year, \$2,649bn of them against \$584bn of every wage ever paid — and it was given somewhere to go: the coupon paid home, a wealth term in the plan, cars, boutiques and kitchens. Net worth oscillates now instead of climbing (432 → 137 → 128 → 214 months of GDP), and the default seed ends on 22 September with the households holding US\$197bn abroad against \$73.8bn at home, and on 28 September US\$356bn against \$60.6bn, where one seed used to hold US\$1.1tn against \$105bn. What is left: a quarter of every plan is never delivered and the undelivered quarter is the hoard, because the city cannot sell its households what they already want to buy; and `MARGINAL_PROPENSITY` has no life-cycle behind it — a fifth of discretionary income saved for ever, by everybody, at every age, is the third leak and the only one entirely untouched. |
| A lockup | The smallest prison is 300 cells for $360M; a city of 15,000 needs about twenty cells. No seed of that size built one, so 2,100–2,900 people were caught over 333 years and every one of them walked — and the cities are ten times the size now: 59,189 caught on the default seed on 22 September, all of them walking, with three stations covering 46% at the end. On 28 September the advisor built jails at last, four of them standing at the end with 344 people inside, and still 35,279 of the 79,592 caught over the run were not held. A 40-cell lockup, or cells in the headquarters, is what is left to decide. |
| Rent per cell should follow the door | The housing match bills landlords by unit size and puts a pensioner in the smallest flat that fits; the household books still charge families and the retired the city's *average* door. So **Senior living alone** is the one cell in trouble in every seed — −\$46 to −\$294 a month for the first decade, \$8,970 owed at the ceiling, locked out — and since the sixth band, **Elder living alone** beside it is the one to watch first when senior care is short. The people outside the families already pay their own door share; families and pensioners do not. |
| The shelf price still has a floor doing a price's job | Retail's cost-plus shelf price cannot fall below a founding constant. The shelf is thirteen invoices now rather than one, so the cost side is real in a way it was not — but the floor is unchanged, and it is still a constant doing a price's job and still part of why the price index cannot fall past about 0.78. It is also half of why the policy rate cannot reach the index; the other half is the row on the shelf and money below. |
| Full general care is worth less than it was | A fully served adult used to die at 0.15% a year. They now die at 0.232% — the halved base rate plus a sliver of illness — because the ×3 swing is gone. The halving does not make up for the good end. The lever is the halving, not the ring. |
| The investment planner ignores every ratio | In most sectors it costs a new building at nameplate capacity — real estate is the exception and the pattern to copy. It also under-builds shops, and it has never built a college, so the student machinery is only exercised in a harness — and, since 0.6.9, in a playtest that is told to build schools (`-Dplaytest.schools=true`). |
| The supply wall | Why can the shops fill only three quarters of a plan in a city with a hundred billion of unspent demand standing in front of them? Retail's binding constraint is coverage times the operating rate, and the operating rate in the default playtest is about half. On the default seed on 22 September the shops fill **77% of the queue they could serve at all**, running at 77%, and the city gets 4.2% of the groceries it asks for, and on 28 September 54%, running at 54%, and 2.5%; whatever is not delivered is banked, by construction, because the settle has nowhere else to put it. The kitchens are a second door and took median hunger from 36% to 22%. The dearer basket — a rich household buying a dearer basket rather than more of them, since nobody eats twice — is the only consumption item left, and Jerus's call was to take it through the new sectors first. |
| Who is playing | The playtest's advisor built five wind farms and two cemeteries for 176,000 people over three centuries, not because it ranks constraints badly but because the loop skips six to a hundred and twenty months between looks, averaging fifty-four — deliberately, the length a person actually clicks. So **every number the harness has ever reported was measured in a city in crisis from neglect**. A second player, `-Dplaytest.player=attentive`, checks in yearly with the same advice: over eight seeds **418,948 people against 148,479, $2,125M a month against $544M**, hunger 18% against 43%, sickness 7.8% against 23.1% — and a labour ceiling the neglected city never reached, at 89% fill. The default is bit-identical to before the flag, so every ensemble in the record stays comparable. And one that cannot be explained: over 600 months the *neglected* city ends bigger and richer than the attentive one while being sicker and hungrier, and over 4,000 the ordering reverses decisively. Something about the early game. And the stand-in player falls behind on police late in a run: that, through crime and migration, is why the default city ended a few percent smaller on 0.7.11, and in 0.7.14's runs every seed that ended with police coverage of 40% or more had 5 to 19 points more unemployment. |
| Bounded world demand | An unbounded export market at a fixed floor means the single best export is built for ever and nothing else ever is: 179 Fabrication Works and zero Machine Works over a run, then nineteen Locomotive Works and two hundred and forty Commercial Vehicle Plants the day those could be sold abroad. The narrow fix was to say the world does not buy vans or wagon sets; the general fix touches four sectors and would change every existing city, and it is still its own batch. |
| Shells, and a banned firm | A sector with no plant can keep a dust of debt and a pantry it can neither use nor sell for up to 3,200 months, defaulting on its interest every month — 78–96% of all the defaults for want of cash on 0.7.12, and little money, and 1,276 of 1,535 on the default seed on 28 September. Nothing winds it up, where a real company in that state is liquidated. And a banned firm with an empty till cannot restock, because the ban shuts the working-capital line the rules keep open for everyone else. |
| Output does not read its inputs | A maker's output does not read the inputs it bought, so holding its inputs to what it can pay for would make goods out of nothing — on 0.7.12's runs it would have skipped $393B of inputs with the same output — and a maker's inputs are bought whole for that reason. A production recipe would be a sixth throttle beside the five ratios (Jerus: *"Buy inputs whole, todo"*). |
| Where the companies' spare cash goes | By `OutwardInvestment`'s rule, mostly abroad: after 0.7.12's eight default runs the companies held $6.7T abroad against $1.7T in their tills, and 26–32% of the bonds; on the default seed on 28 September they ended with $928bn abroad against $233bn in their tills. And the household cells' rebalancing on the book barely fires, $0.47M offered over eight runs, because a cell short of money has usually sold in its waterfall already. |
| The young bank, and a plant that loses money before interest | Under every failure 0.7.8 left, one sector held 30–73% of the book, and since 0.7.12 concentration is priced rather than capped (answered below). What still fails the bank is the young one, on the $32M of capital its founding branch brings, before month 1,000, when Manufacturing or Automotive goes under; a plant retired at material price can take a sector past the line within months, and on autopilot seed 7 a $44M backstop met a $21M bank. The last change of 0.7.12 took the autopilot's failures from 4 to 9, and that was not traced. The single-industry multiplier the price uses is Basel III's 1.25, set for large financial institutions, and is kept and flagged; and branch openings between the minimum and the target, 35% of the default runs' openings on 0.7.11, leave the old trap of recapitalising a bank by opening branches open in that band. The row that stood here, *a plant that loses money before interest is still lent for*, now meets a price off the curve at the leverage the plant would leave the sector at (0.7.8) and a door shut past the default point (0.7.12); it has not been measured again since 0.7.2. |
| The default curve's one number | `BusinessDebtManager.ASSET_VOLATILITY` 0.25, the spread of fortunes among a sector's firms, from the Merton and KMV literature's 20–35% and not tuned to any result: at 0.20 the curve is steeper, fewer defaults under the line and more past it, and at 0.35 flatter. Jerus's to settle. |
| The bank's target sits at its cap | `Bank.MAX_BUFFER` binds in every seed: the worst year a bank lives through was 38–109% of its weighted book on 0.7.8's runs, so its target is 16.5% throughout and covers a sixth of it. On the default seed on 28 September the worst year on record was 12.06% of the book, and the target 16.5%. |
| The quarter prices the shortfall desk past the default point | The shortfall desk lends on the month's leverage while the price reads the quarter, which was Jerus's choice, so over 0.7.8's default eight 1,435 of its loans were priced past the default point, 73% of them Luxury Retail in the high month of its restock. Pricing the shortfall desk on the month, or on the lower of the two, would stop it, and it is his call. On 28 September 16 loans were written past the default point over the run. |
| Deposits are not on the bank's books | The bank counts the city's savings as deposits for its capacity without holding them, the one stated simplification in its header. It is the root of the worst stress finding of 0.7.7 — held at 10%, a recovered bank paid savers its chosen 3.5% over the world's 2%, the households brought US$2.7bn home into a city of about 2,000, and prices ran to 5.64 times founding before they unwound — and the reason the Balance sheet page carries deposits as a memo line. Putting them on the books moves the bank's three statements, the audit's pools, every payment between a household and a business and the central bank's interest on reserves, and it is its own batch (Jerus: *"Memo now, own batch later"*). |
| The city keeps its bank | A resolved bank's stake falls only as it sells new shares (Jerus: *"New issues only"*), so the city keeps its bank for decades: a median 58.8% twenty-five years after a default resolution, and 91–100% in the autopilot and held setups (0.7.14). A sell-down like the United Kingdom's out of NatWest, by placements, a trading plan and directed buybacks from 2015 to 2025, is Jerus's if he wants one; the player can sell the rescue book by hand. Beside it: the fund never pays for a rescue, by his word, and at a 300% dial all 66 months on advances were resolutions' while the fund held about $500B; it can pass 10% of a company without buying when that company's buybacks shrink the shares under it; and TARP's $25B cap is left out, because nothing converts it into this game's money. |
| The landlords' test is per building | So a landlord whose profit is under its mortgages' principal borrows the difference from the shortfall desk — $1.46B on one seed of 0.7.11 — and the 10% city's insurance losses came from the same place. And a landlord with an empty till can wait on its 15% down payment: 250 months on 0.7.12's seed 5, with households there going without a home for 161 of them. |
| Size-level slack in the housing retirement rule | A distressed landlord sold 5,800 of 13,272 homes in seven months because the rule asked whether the segment had spare doors and the slack was spread over four sizes. Guarded — nobody sells a door while somebody has nowhere — not fixed. Whether a given set of households fits a given set of doors is a packing question and no comparison of totals answers it. |
| Every planner assumes the ground is free | The fields plan off the crop market, the houses off the jobs, the fabricators off the steel price, the railway off the freight nobody is carrying, and none of them can see that they are bidding for the same land. The rule that stopped the farms crowding out housing is a patch on one sector, not a mechanism, and the railway and the assembly plants are the hungriest for ground the game has had. A land market the planners bid into. |
| Converting for land does not push the currency | The 0.7.6 brief asked that whatever pressure the exchange puts on the rate when the treasury buys dollars apply to land too, and there is none to apply: a treasury purchase of dollars is the financing item below the line, which the pressure never reads, so buying reserves has never moved the rate and `ForeignCheck`'s section 14 asserts an equality with nothing. Right for reserves, whose dollars stay in the country; arguably wrong for land, which the world sold the city and was paid for in dollars the city had to buy, so a city that spends a decade buying ground sees no weakening for it. The fix is small — count the dollars paid abroad for land as an outflow the pressure reads, for converting or for both — and it is Jerus's call. |
| A third of meals out, and two businesses that cannot fail | `MOST_MEALS_EATEN_OUT` is a third and nothing measures whether that is the right number; on the best seeds a quarter of the city eats out and the kitchens build to the cap. Restaurants finish seven seeds of eight with zero write-downs at 2.00% credit, the profile of Retail and Agriculture, the sectors that have never gone under — a business that cannot fail is not much of a decision. Luxury Retail is the opposite, going under more often than anything but Mining and Materials, its two buildings never sized against a city's luxury budget, and **it still has no harness of its own**: every bootstrap fault the kitchens hit had already been paid for there, and nothing names `Automotive` either. |
| A car costs nothing to keep, and its loan is a bridge | Jerus wants a car to cost something to keep, which gives *cut back expenses* something to cut and makes a financed car a real commitment; the open question is where the money lands — rent reaches Real Estate through a good and a sale, so a motoring bill needs a new good sold by Automotive, or fuel imported from the world. And a car loan with a term, if the credit cycle is meant to be felt rather than merely recorded: today's loan is repaid out of spare cash within a month or two. |
| The railway's allowed return is a constant | A regulated network's allowed return follows the cost of its money; here `TARGET_RETURN` is 1.2% a month whatever the credit desk charges, and the link runs the other way — dear money keeps the band wide. Alongside it: the railway settles at 38–43% of the lorry rate in the ensemble and has been seen quoting 99% of a lorry, which leaves shippers barely better off; and rail haulage does not reduce a sector's van need, while Construction draws its materials on demand and so reads as moving nothing. |
| What no harness looks at | The sector pages are the only screen whose text a harness reads. The city panel, the People screen, the Policy pages and the Reports page are as right as somebody's last look at them; the Infrastructure tab shipped without anyone looking at it and its layout pass is owed — a twelfth tab crowding the rail on a short window, five-column tables wider than the statement column; and the four opening statement lines build nodes directly rather than lines a check can read. The screens cannot run in the cloud, so they are checked by eye on the PC, and those of 0.7.2 to 0.7.15 have not been, bar 0.7.10's founding screen, which Jerus checked on 24 September. Still to look at: the strip's three panels and its colours from the target, the Money page and the monetary page with the target's, the holdings' and the ceiling's ladders; the sector list's sparklines and the tax pages' own bases (0.7.4); the Reports page — its pins, its two axes, the crosshair, the bands and the episodes — and Enter and Backspace on a build page (0.7.5); every ladder, the school rows, the Reports page's GDP layers and the land office's two ways to pay (0.7.6); prime and the savers' share where the bank's premium used to show — on the Summary, the Finances rate page, the sector page, the Policy page and the strip's tooltip (0.7.7); the Bank tab, rebuilt and grown since (0.7.7 to 0.7.9, 0.7.11, 0.7.13, 0.7.14); the Real Estate screen's mortgages and the Government tab's premiums and claims (0.7.11); the bond market, the Sector page's owners' book, a household's bonds and the interim financing (0.7.12); the land office in km², its funding page and *Buy the next N*, and the rollover's block (0.7.13); the city's fund, the rescue setting, the preferred offer and the Insane card (0.7.14); and the target's ladder to 20%, the holdings ladder to 100%, the rollover's central bank lines and the skip report's advances (0.7.15). `BankCheck` asserts the Bank tab's arithmetic, not its drawing, and every screen but the Bank tab snaps an opened line shut on the month's redraw. Education's cost and the transit payroll are outside G, which healthcare's and the police's are not. |
| Two small calls from 0.7.4 | Whether the inflation target should be staged and applied with the rate, rather than taking effect at once as the ceiling does; and whether the bank should have its own row on the profit tax page, since it is taxed at retail's rate and nothing on the screen says so. |
